title: Jaguars NFL Trade Deadline Big Board: Who Still Fits With One Week Left?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is never too early to look ahead.
While the Jacksonville Jaguars sit atop the AFC South thanks to their 5-2 start, that does not mean the Jaguars can't still improve. And the easiest way to do that would be by utilizing next week's trade deadline.
The 2026 trade deadline is just seven days away, and here is an updated big board of targets worth pursuing.
The Fit: I have talked before about why I think Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo is a great fit for the Jaguars. Ojomo is strong against the run, has produced at a high-level as a pass-rusher before, and has the type of explosive skill-set that the Jaguars need to add to their interior defensive line moving forward. Ojomo may be not be a scale-tipper by himself, but he would be a quality add considering his ability to be disruptive and win one-on-ones.
The Cost: This is interesting. If he was under contract for a few more years, it would likely be a Day 2 pick. The fact he is a rental, though, suggests to me he could be had for a Day 3 pick if the Eagles continue to lose games. He would cost virtually nothing in terms of cap space, but if he hits free agency in March he would likely net the Jaguars a comp pick. If the Eagles go into sell mode, I think you could get Ojomo for something perhaps even less than what the Jaguars gave up last year for a then-rental of Jakobi Meyers, who cost a fourth- and a sixth-round pick.
The Fit: Christian Barmore is more of a three-technique than a true nose tackle, though he does have more run-defending ability than people give him credit for. He has not been very productive this season, but he does have a long history of providing an interior pass-rush that would boost the Jaguars' defense.
The Price: Reports are that Barmore would cost a Day 3 pick, which makes sense considering his reduced role and injury history. He is worth the swing for a team like the Jaguars that must do anything they can to keep their window open.
The Fit: There are two defensive tackles worth considering here: Derrick Brown and Bobby Brown. Each would thrive as a nose tackle in the Jaguars' scheme, though Derrick Brown is clearly the bigger name and more high-ceiling option. Bobby Brown did start his career with the Los Angeles Rams while James Gladstone was there, though.
The Price: Derrick Brown would likely cost a third-round pick at the absolute lowest, though a second-round pick would be more likely. He has a big contract attached to him, which does complicate it. I would imagine that Bobby Brown could be had for a sixth- or seventh-round pick as his role has been somewhat reduced.
The Fit: Another player who makes sense for the Jaguars to go after following Davon Hamilton's season-ending injury is Roy Lopez, who has quietly been one of the more well-balanced and productive defensive tackles in football this season. He could start at nose tackle while also giving the Jaguars some pass-rush juice inside.
The Price: The Cardinals are a losing football team in the best division in football. It would make little sense for them to not be open to dealing Lopez, who is on a cheap, short deal. A mid-to-late Day 3 pick would make sense for all parties here.
The Fit: This one is easy in the wake of DaVon Hamilton's season-ending injury. Tomlinson has been a force against the run throughout his long NFL career and he would be able to slot in as the Jaguars' space eater right off the bat. The Jaguars do not have another body type in their defensive tackle room like Hamilton, but Tomlinson would check that box.
The Price: With the Chargers sitting at 0-7 and Tomlinson on a one-year deal, the Chargers would be wise to take a ham sandwhich for Tomlinson. A seventh-round pick should be able to get this done every time.
The Fit: I mean, this one is obvious. Travon Walker has had a really good season, but imagine adding Khalil Mack to the mix with him and Josh Hines-Allen and allowing Walker to get more rush snaps inside at defensive tackle. A third-down rush package with Hines-Allen and Mack on the edges and Walker and Arik Armstead inside would be very effective, and Mack would clearly welcome joining a team with deep playoff run aspirations as opposed to whatever is going on in Los Angeles.
The Cost: It has been reported that the Chargers would likely take a fifth-round pick for Mack, which is a deal I think the Jaguars would be comfortable making in a big way. The Jaguars have been very willing to deal Day 3 picks over the last two years because they know they can restock the picks with the compensatory draft pick formula, so this feels like it would be an easy decision for the Jaguars to make. The Chargers just keep losing games, and Mack is one of the players who is the clearest trade candidate.
The Fit: I have mentioned in the past that I am a big fan of Miami Dolphins defensive tackle Zach Sieler, who does have a connection with a few different coaches on the Jaguars' staff. Sieler is not the pass-rusher he used to be, but he does make a ton of plays in the middle of the defensive line, is willing to handle the dirty work, and would fit right in with the brand of defense the Jaguars play. There are better pass-rushers, but he would still give the Jaguars quite the boost when it comes to the trenches in December, January and deep into the playoffs as well.
The Cost: You probably do not feel great if you have to give up more than a fifth for Sieler at this stage of his career, but a fourth and a future pick like they did for Jakobi Meyers would fit into the Jaguars' draft ammo, too. The Dolphins are going to keep losing games, butit does remain to be seen how quickly they will truly give up on this season.

title: Jaguars-Ravens Injury Report: Bhayshul Tuten's Injury Could Mean Larger Role For 1 Veteran
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have quite the lengthy injury report ahead of their Thursday Night Football matchup with the Baltimore Ravens, but there is one name that jumps off the page.
Jaguars running back Bhayshul Tuten did not practice Tuesday as the result of an ankle/foot injury. Tuten was also listed as a non-participant in the walkthrough on the practice field Monday, with that day's injury report being just an estimate.
With Tuten's status seemingly up in the air ahead of the Week 9 clash with the Ravens, the Jaguars might have to pivot and turn to one player to step up in his potential abscence: veteran running back Chris Rodriguez Jr.
Rodriguez himself was limited in Tuesday's practice with a hand injury, but that doesn't take away from the fact that he would be the expected bell cow of the offense if Tuten can't play. Tuten has played a massive role in the offense through the first seven games, getting more carries than Rodriguez in every game but one (Week 6).
But with Tuten banged up on a short week, the Jaguars may hesitate to fully deploy their rising star. Tuten is fresh off the best game of his career, but the Jaguars need him much more down the stretch than they should need him to beat a 4-4 Ravens team on Thursday Night Football considering they are down to their third-string quarterback.
Rodriguez has quietly been one of the most efficient running backs in football over the first half of the season. According to NextGenStats, he ranks No. 3 among all running backs in EPA/attempt and No. 5 in success rate. Part of this is likely due to the fact that he is the Jaguars' short-yardage back, thus giving him shorter downs and distances to get a first down, but he has always been an efficient runner. The Jaguars are simply the ones benefitting from, it now.
Rodriguez has 45 carries for 209 yards (4.6 yards per carry) and three touchdowns this season, scoring two rushing touchdowns from 20+ yards out. This included a 28-yard touchdown in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts, with Rodriguez and Tuten each taking a step forward in giving the Jaguars the explosive rushing game they have been looking for.
“It's there. I mean, just watch the film, like, it's there. There's been plenty of times where me and Bhayshul [Tuten] have talked, and we're like, man, if we just slowed down a little bit or had a bit more patience, or if we would have read it out all the way through the guy and not just reading our first read, but our second read, man, we'll have so many explosives," Rodriguez said about the explosive runs during the bye week.
"And we talked about it today. There are so many yards that we left out there in this past game. It's over, we can't get them back, but the only thing we can do is learn from it and move on.”
Rodriguez found those missing yards against the Colts. If they are without Tuten on Thursday night, they will need him to find a lot more.

title: Jaguars NFL Trade Deadline Rumors Tracker: Latest News, Targets and Updates
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL Trade deadline is just seven days away, and it sure feels like the Jacksonville Jaguars are a team to watch.
The Jaguars have been one of the more active teams in terms of trades since hiring general manager James Gladstone, including one trade deadline move last year to land wide receiver Jakobi Meyers. The last few weeks have been about identifying which targets might be next for the Jaguars to take a look at.
With recent injuries to Eric Murray and Davon Hamilton potentially making the Jaguars' moves even more urgent, here is a running tracker on each piece of information flying out there about the Jaguars right now.
Do not forget to keep checking back here as each situation develops ahead of next week's deadline, either.
The latest report from ESPN's Jeremy Fowler has a few connections for the Jaguars to one key potential trade piece: defensive tackle Moro Ojomo, the rising Philadelphia Eagles defender who is due to cash in when it comes to free agency next March. We have discussed Ojomo before, and now the Jaguars have been officially tied to him.
"Jacksonville is looking and willing to be aggressive for defensive line help. It would have heavily pursued Simmons last week if it weren't in the same division as the Titans, Simmons' old team. Now, Simmons is a unique case -- no other available player is like him. But the point stands that Jacksonville could make a move for a key player at the right price ... Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo is a person of interest here, though Philly is inclined to keep and potentially extend him," Fowler said.
Fowler later discussed the Jaguars as a key team of interest when it came to his notes on Ojomo's general market. It is looking more and more like he could be a real option for Jacksonville, which could depend on the Eagles losing this Sunday.
According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, the Jaguars are hunting some big game along the defensive line. This would track with reports over the last week-plus that defensive line is where the Jaguars' primary area of focus is entering the trade deadline week.
"My understanding is the Jacksonville Jaguars and James Gladstone, the general manager, have been working the phones over the last several days targeting a top-tier defensive lineman. Will they get one? We don't know," Rapoport said. "I know Jeff Simmons was someone they were interested. They never going to do that in the division, but certainly, especially losing Devon Hamilton, big run stuffer and a menace in the middle. That is an area of need for them."
"Brian Thomas Jr. has been the area of interest for a lot of other teams." @RapSheet provides updates on the Jags' potential moves ahead of the trade deadline ✍️ pic.twitter.com/nbOAO2RNxz
With Simmons and Buckner already traded and with Daron Payne on injured reserve , there is some serious question of who the top-tier defensive linemen would be on the market. Philadelphia Eagles' defensive tackle Moro Ojomo is the first name that comes to mind, though New England Patriots' Christian Barmore could qualify. And what about Carolina Panthers star Derrick Brown? He was commonly mocked to the Jaguars during the 2020 NFL Draft process, and that would be a full-circle move.
This has been a situation worth monitoring for some time now. It remains to be seen if the Jaguars actually want to move Thomas. Most reports have been clear: the Jaguars have been reluctant to engage in any talks about Thomas, which has been the team's stance since Thomas' name first got floated out around this time a year ago. The Ringer's Tom Pelissero reported over the weekend that some believe the Jaguars' stance will change, but it feels unlikely the Jaguars feel any differently about Thomas now than they did when they refused to make a move in the past.
The Jaguars have been fending off trade interest in WR Brian Thomas Jr. for over a year. But the former first-round pick’s recent benching and ongoing struggles have ramped up belief within the league that Jacksonville will move him by the deadline. More in The Sweep:… pic.twitter.com/3L1E0V8kk9
NBC's Mike Florio has reported the teams that seem to have interest in Thomas: the Washington Commanders, the Kansas City Chiefs, and the Pittsburgh Steelers. He noted that the Steelers and Chiefs each also like Josh Downs, while noting that the Steelers prefer Downs and the Chiefs prefer Thomas. Meanwhile, the Commanders are led on offense by Thomas' former college quarterback in Jayden Daniels.
There has not yet been any reporting that indicates the Jaguars are actively seeking to trade Thomas, though the Athletic's Jonathan Jones said the Jaguars have "been firm" that they are not seeking to trade him. Jones also noted that if Thomas was traded, he would likely only be had for a Day 2 pick.
The Jaguars have been connected to the defensive tackle market for a few weeks now, and the latest such reporting is from Ian Rapoport. The NFL Network insider pointed the Jaguars and Minnesota Vikings out as teams that are looking for defensive tackle help at the deadline, which made sense for the Jaguars before Hamilton's season-ending injury. Now that Hamilton is out, the need for a defensive tackle has been raised.
Trade deadline temperature check with @RapSheet on Colts, RBs, Eagles, Chargers. pic.twitter.com/0VVe8IK3dL
Rapoport is not the first to connect the Jaguars to defensive tackle help, either. SI's Albert Breer reported a week ago the Jaguars were looking for help along the interior defensive line, and even Jaguars general manager James Gladstone had some interesting remarks to make when it came to recent defensive tackle deals within the AFC South. If the Jaguars add a player, it feels like it would be here at ths spot.

title: Jaguars Have 3 Trade Suitors Emerging for Brian Thomas Jr.: Who Makes the Most Sense?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a week left to make a big decision, and it is starting to become clear which teams might help them make that decision when it comes to Brian Thomas Jr.
With the way the Jaguars deployed Thomas in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts, perhaps the Jaguars will not even move the third-year receiver during his streak of iffy production. But if the Jaguars do deal him, ProFootballTalk's Mike Florio says there are three teams that have been connected to the star wideout.
"Currently, the Chiefs, Steelers, and Commanders have interest. The Steelers, we’re told, have greater interest in Colts receiver Josh Downs. Downs, however, is Kansas City’s Plan B, if they can’t get Thomas away from the Jaguars," Florio reported this week.
So, which of these teams make the most sense if the Jaguars do move on from Thomas? We review each case below.
We noted the Washington Commanders as the top logical fit for Thomas in October, and it is easy to see why. The Commanders are ... maybe still in it in a really bad NFC East. But they badly need wide receiver help after the season-ending injury to Terry McLaurin a few weeks ago. The Commanders needed to add to their receiver room maybe more than any other team this offseason and their solutions were Antonio Williams, a perfectly fine rookie slot receiver, and an aging Stefon Diggs.
There is also the quarterback connection. Thomas was a top target for Jayden Daniels during his time at LSU, and the two are clearly close even since entering the NFL for different franchises. The Houston Texans added Marvin Harrison Jr. for his college quarterback in CJ Stroud, so it would make sense for the Commanders to do the same with Daniels. The move could not just help the Commanders in the short-term, either, since Thomas could be seen as a long-term WR1 if everything pans out.
This would have made even more sense for Daron Payne was injured, but the Commanders are still, to me, the most likely landing spot for Thomas if the Jaguars do move on. It is becoming a bit more unlikely the Jaguars do that, but this is the team I think is worth watching.
The Pittsburgh Steelers are, speaking in technical terms, contenders in the AFC along with the Jaguars. Trading a star player and an explosive play-maker like Thomas to a fellow AFC team that is pushing for a high seed in the playoffs would not exactly be ideal, but I believe the Steelers could sweeten the terms to make it worth the Jaguars' while. That is, of course, if the Steelers feel desperate enough.
The Steelers do not have all that much firepower on offense, and could see Thomas as a way to compete with the Cincinnati Bengals for the AFC North crown. There are likely better fits for the way Aaron Rodgers plays and what kind of offense the Steelers run, such as Josh Downs, but they still badly need wide receiver help. For the right package, this would make sense.
If I had to guess which team would be willing to pay the highest price for Thomas, it would probably be the Kansas City Chiefs. The Chiefs do not have any speed or big-play threat at wide receiver outside of Xavier Worthy, who has proven to be a below-average receiver during his NFL career. The Chiefs have been looking to replace Tyreek Hill for years, and Thomas has the speed and big-play ability to give them that.
With that said, the Chiefs are an AFC contender that the Jaguars likely would not want to help improve all that much. There is a strong chance the Jaguars would have to beat the Chiefs at some point with Thomas on their roster, and the Jaguars clearly think Thomas is a very talented wideout. They would not want to see that kind of talent across from them in a big game, I would imagine.

title: 3 Things We Learned From the Jaguars' Week 8 Win Over the Colts: Hope For Brian Thomas Jr.
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have a quick turnaround before Week 9's Thursday Night Football clash with the Baltimore Ravens, but there is still time to take a few more peeks at their dominant Week 8.
The Jaguars absolutely dismantled the Indianapolis Colts in Jacksonville, the continuation of what has been a decade-plus of ending the Colts' season inside the walls of EverBank Stadium. But what did we learn from the latest version of the Jaguars taking care of business against the Colts? We break it down below.
The Jaguars did not give up on Brian Thomas Jr. during the bye week. It seemed like there was a very real chance of this happening after he was benched during the second-half of the Week 6 loss to the Houston Texans in London, but the Jaguars had Thomas out there with the rest of the starting offense every time they went to three-wide receiver sets. This culminated in Thomas catching a red-zone touchdown from Trevor Lawrence to make it a 7-0 game, the first of six touchdowns the Jaguars would score on Sunday.
“He's a young dude but he's very mature. He's not an immature guy that you're emotional and gets too high and too low. And he said it, I think last week, he's going to continue to come out and do his job. And I think I said at some point last week that he was going to make plays for us in this game, and we all had belief that that was going to happen, and we're going to continue to believe that," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday. "We're going to continue to work with him and continue to try to get the most out of every player, especially B.T. But I have been impressed with the way that he's able to block out the noise, continue to be integrated with everybody. I was proud. I was very happy for him to see him make that play on the first drive of the game on a critical third-and-goal to go.”
The Jaguars could have easily sat Thomas on the sidelines once more, especially in a run-heavy game where they could have reasoned that two-tight end sets and Josh Cameron were more appropriate to have on the field. Instead, the Jaguars let Thomas play quite a bit and he was targeted twice on Trevor Lawrence's 14 attempts. Only Jakobi Meyers got targeted more on Sunday, making it clear that while the Jaguars still weigh the Thomas trade market, they are not about to simply give up on the former first-round pick.
The Jaguars had a number of key depth pieces step up in big ways on Sunday: Rayuan Lane with a pick-six, Branson Combs with an interception and several big special teams plays, Matt Dickerson stepping in after Davon Hamilton's injury, Wyatt Milum filling in at right guard for an injured Ezra Cleveland, and so on and so forth. It was a good sign to see the Jaguars' depth play well, and we now know they are going to need them more than ever due to the season-ending injuries to Hamilton and Eric Murray.
"I do believe we have really good leadership. It's going to be tested now more than ever, with D-Ham and Eric Murray specifically, two veteran football players, starters. Not only that, but unbelievable human beings and leaders on this football team. We're going to be tested this week for sure," Coen said. "Our mental toughness will be tested, our group collaboration and connectivity will be tested, but fully anticipate this group to be able to connect and stay together.”
How the Jaguars' depth handles those tests will tell us whether the Jaguars can sustain their injuries moving forward. The Jaguars have lost three starters to season-ending injuries over the last three games with Hamilton, Murray, and left tackle Anton Harrison. We found out during Week 8 what the Jaguars' depth is capable of, and now we will find out if they can keep meeting the challenge.
The Jaguars utilized a cornerback rotation during the first three weeks of the season that proved to be effective, largely because it allowed the Jaguars to deploy Jarrian Jones in his more natural position in the slot. Jones only played 12 snaps in the blowout win, though he is listed with an ankl;e injury on this week's injury report. But we saw Jones play in the slot on the second drive of the game and make a clear impact on the secondary.
The only reason the Jaguars were able to do this was due to the return of Brown. When the Jaguars did not have Brown on the field over the last few weeks due to his hamstring injury, they had to play with a cornerback set up that they clearly were not overly comfortable with. Now that Brown is back in the mix, the Jaguars have their ideal cornerback set-up.
"It definitely helped having him back, that's for sure," Coen said. "It just gives us more flexibility to do different things with Jarrian [CB Jarrian Jones] and J-Lew [CB Jourdan Lewis] and Travis as well. You need corners. They always get nicked up. It's just the name of the game, it's the nature of how it goes. You can never have enough good corners in this league. Really glad to have Buster back, absolutely."

title: What's Going On With R Mason Thomas?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' pass rush has struggled so far this season, and if you've been watching the unit particularly closely, you may be ready to argue that "has struggled" is an understatement.
The Chiefs did not record a sack in four of their first seven games of this season, and their only sack against the Denver Broncos in Week 8 was aided by Bo Nix short-circuiting when he spiked the ball behind him while under pressure. (By the way, that play was one of only two total times Nix was pressured on Sunday.)
ESPN Research: Chiefs pressured Bo Nix on 2 of 34 dropbacks (6%), the lowest for any team since 2024 Week 5, and the lowest for the Chiefs since 2012 Week 8 Chiefs had a 48.5% pressure rate on Nix in Week 1
George Karlaftis has recorded two sacks this season. No other Chief has more than one. Chris Jones hasn't recorded a box score stat in two weeks —a remarkable fact even as he still faces more than his fair share of double-teams. Second-year third-round pick Ashton Gillotte is establishing himself as a solid player, but not a disruptive pass-rusher. Former first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah showed some flashes through the first few weeks, recording a sack in Week 1 and four quarterback hits through the first five games of the year , but he's been quieter since the bye week.
Most of those players currently feel like relatively straightforward known quantities. Good players! But largely already defined in their role for an NFL rotation. That's part of what makes rookie second-round pick R Mason Thomas so alluring, and also what makes his last two weeks so confusing.
Through the first five games of the season, Thomas played between 41.5% and 59.5% of the team's defensive snaps , with a few splash plays to show for it. Against the Seahawks, he played only 29% (20 snaps). In Denver, just 27% (17 snaps). Why the decrease in the last two games?
While this year's No. 40 overall pick has certainly had his share of poor snaps against the run , Seattle and Denver were both struggling to move the ball on the ground before their matchups with the Chiefs, and Thomas was given a larger workload at the very beginning of his NFL career, including in KC's Week 1 win over Denver when he played 27 snaps (53%) against those same Broncos.
To be fair, Thomas' workload has decreased, not disappeared, in the last two weeks. Still, it's hard to find a logical reason for him to be taken off the field as often as he has been.
Sure, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo often prefers veteran players in a vacuum, and he seems to have a penchant for bigger edge defenders who can be trusted to stay stout against the run—again, not Thomas' strength. But the Chiefs specifically need quick pressures from their four-man rush, which is something that Thomas can provide.
Thomas has played 17 fewer defensive snaps than Gillotte and 29 fewer than Anudike-Uzomah this season, which is still a substantial sample size for the rookie. In that time, according to Next Gen Stats , Thomas has led the Chiefs in pressure rate by a substantial margin.
Chiefs leaders in QB pressure rate through 7 games ( @NextGenStats ) R Mason Thomas (17%) George Karlaftis (12%) FAU (9.6%) Ashton Gillotte (7.5%) Khyiris Tonga (7.1%) Chris Jones (6.7%) Peter Woods (2.2%)
There's room for all of these players in Kansas City's struggling defensive line rotation. Gillotte can keep his running-down snaps. Karlaftis is strong on his edge. Anudike-Uzomah has also been rushing from the interior. Across the board, Kansas City needs more ways to pressure the quarterback, and Thomas' skill set is completely unique on this roster.
Thomas is not perfect. He's not a finished product. I'm not even calling him the best defensive end on the team—that title still belongs to Karlaftis and his well-rounded suite of tools. But as all eyes turn to the NFL's trade deadline, I still believe that the Chiefs' best chance for a second-half pass-rushing resurgence comes with a larger dose of Thomas. He should be given every opportunity to learn and get after the quarterback here in his rookie season, with hopes of his game coming together in time for the playoff push.
. @ByNateTaylor cooking on @ChiefsHMA “R Mason Thomas in 81 plays as a pass rusher has 20 wins. Ranks 13th in pass rush win rate when giving true chances to rush the passer in dropback settings.”
Again, this is currently still a short-term issue that could end up being just a two-game blip on the radar. I don't believe that Thomas has been soft-benched by Spagnuolo, sent to the doghouse, been entirely demoted, or anything of that sort. But those recent snap counts should still be a wake-up call for the Chiefs' defensive coaching staff. If Thomas can stumble into an insignificant workload just because of the flow of a particular game, they need to make a concerted effort to be sure it doesn't happen again.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: What Could Kansas City Realistically Do at the Trade Deadline?
full_text:
After back-to-back frustrating losses—a blowout in Seattle and a meltdown in Denver —the Kansas City Chiefs are in a strange place. They're still clearly among the contenders in the AFC , but that's part of the strange feeling surrounding Chiefs Kingdom. They're among the rest of the contenders, not rising to a tier above them.
With a week until the NFL's trade deadline, what could the Chiefs do to bolster their roster in the next seven days, and where does the team stand now? That's what we'll unpack in today's Chiefs On SI mailbag.
In your opinion, what trades or position upgrades should the Chiefs make at the deadline? And realistically, which ones will they actually make? What’s your gut saying? - @MrEd315
The Chiefs clearly haven't gotten enough out of their pass catchers or pass rushers so far this season, so that's the place to begin. On the defensive line, however, I don't know if there's an external option that truly makes sense.
I'd be surprised to see the Chiefs make a huge swing for a player like Josh Sweat unless his price tag is much lower than expected, and if they look for a lower-tier player, they have to be an improvement (and earn Steve Spagnuolo's trust) over players like Felix Anudike-Uzomah and Ashton Gillotte, who are having nice seasons so far.
Wide receiver has some openings. I'd keep calling the Colts about Josh Downs until the price drops as far as it'll go, and I'd be interested in Brian Thomas Jr. as a multi-year solution while he's a buy-low candidate. I'd make room for someone like Dontayvion Wicks at a fair price too. There are a few creative mid-level answers out there... but my gut feeling?
My gut feeling is that it might not matter all that much. Andy Reid's comments last week , if taken at face value, remind us that the best chance for an improvement this season may have to come from a player who was on the team in training camp.
What are the top three realistic fixes the Chiefs can make in the middle of this season that give them the best shot to win the Super Bowl? Offensive line help? WR? - @mattlacasse.bsky.social
Since we just talked about trade options, I want to take this question to three internal solutions the Chiefs could find without reaching for outside help.
First, keep ramping up Cyrus Allen's workload. It wasn't perfect on Sunday in Denver, and it won't be perfect in the weeks to come. But he's more dynamic than Jalen Royals or Andrew Armstrong, and Xavier Worthy's apparent mistakes haven't kept him off the field.
Second, lean into the ground-and-pound production we saw during the first several weeks of the season. With Rashee Rice back, the offense should be multidimensional enough to keep defenses guessing, and the under-center offense is worth returning to. Go under center and hand it to Walker. Go under center and run some play-action. These last two weeks have felt like a regression to some of the problems of 2025. (And as a bonus, use that under-center offense to be aggressive on 4th-and-short. No more questionable kicks or unnecessary punts.)
Third, get as many pass-rushing snaps for R Mason Thomas as possible. If the Chiefs' pass rush is going to take a meaningful step forward, I think Thomas would be the most likely candidate for a substantial breakout. The rookie defensive end played a season-low 17 snaps (27%) in Denver after playing a then-low 20 snaps (29%) in Seattle. He doesn't need to be on the field for every likely rushing down, but he needs opportunities to get after the quarterback.
Is there something going on with Chris Jones? Dude's production has completely disappeared. - @ZachTakes
I have been (and still remain) extremely hesitant to sound the alarm on Chris Jones; he's one of the three most important players of the Chiefs' dynasty and has shown an incredible ability to be disruptive, even when facing tremendous attention from opposing offenses. I'm still holding out hope for a late-season/playoff-push stretch of games where Jones turns back the clock, but it's impossible to pretend that he's performing at his usual standard.
I think that's partially the encroachment of Father Time having an impact on the 32-year-old and partially an indictment on the rest of the Chiefs' defensive front, revealing how much they've relied on Jones to be elite for so many years. Still, that doesn't feel like enough to explain the fact that he hasn't recorded a statistic in two weeks . He had a calf issue reported on the Chiefs' injury reports through Week 4, but he's been clear of that designation since the bye.
I still believe that there will be game-changing moments from Jones down the stretch of this season, but I have to acknowledge that it's been a long time since we've seen one.
Did Reid decide to attempt a field goal in the fourth quarter as a way to assess if a change was needed this week?
 - @SoCal1186
I sure hope that wasn't the logic. Even without Harrison Butker's recent history front of mind, kicking a field goal there was the wrong choice. According to Next Gen Stats , punting the ball away in that scenario would have added the most win probability (raising it to 74.3%), while going for it would've put KC's win probability at 72.5%. Attempting the field goal was the least-analytically-sound decision at 71.5%.
If you don't care about analytics, you could rely on the eye test, your gut, and your recent memory to surmise that a 54-yard field goal in the rain was probably not going in from the struggling Butker. If he had hit that field goal, the Broncos would've still had solid starting field position after the kickoff, needing a touchdown to take the lead, and I think Butker would've still needed a few more clean weeks before he could be viewed as "back." However you slice it, I just don't think sending him out there in that scenario was a good decision.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Day 3 Pick on the Rise After Week 8?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs outplayed the Denver Broncos for a huge chunk of their Week 8 meeting, only to give the game away near the end and fail to recover before the clock hit zeroes. That doesn't mean there wasn't plenty of good to take away from the contest, though, particularly regarding the club's young players.
Multiple first and second-year pieces continued to make names for themselves on Sunday, ranging from early-round NFL Draft selections by general manager Brett Veach to lesser-discussed pickups. Where does everyone stand as a new week of play begins?
Following Week 8, let's break down the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each qualifying 53-man roster member in tiers. Be sure to return to this series each week to see who's moving and shaking.
Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott, whose practice window was recently opened , isn't included due to him still being on the physically unable to perform list .
Left tackle Josh Simmons sits this one out after going to injured reserve . The same applies to running back Brashard Smith .
The secondary duo of cornerbacks Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane could be one of the Chiefs' most important tandems for the next couple of years. Williams has certainly held up his end of the bargain this year. Delane missed more time with a lingering shoulder injury , which head coach Andy Reid acknowledged will be a thing for a while.
"It's just a matter of being strong, strong enough to get out there," Reid said on Monday. "So there's a good chance he'll be able to get — or at least a chance — that he'll be able to get himself out there this week. But again, it's just how strong it is. We will see; that's going to be a day-to-day thing. If he can do it, he can do it. If not, (Kristian) Fulton did a nice job in there.”
Second-round defensive end R Mason Thomas had one of Kansas City's many Week 8 penalties, albeit while also recording a batted pass on the Broncos' third drive and continuing to flash plenty of athletic upside. Second-year man Ashton Gillotte, who's come on strong in recent weeks, played terrific run defense all afternoon and into the evening.
The (positive) story of the game, however, was fifth-round running back Emmett Johnson. His 15-yard rush featuring multiple broken tackles and his fourth-quarter kickoff return were both nice, but his value in the passing game managed to outshine everything else. Johnson finished with five receptions for 128 yards and a touchdown, potentially earning an increased role in the process.
Emmett Johnson has been the best RB of Week 8. pic.twitter.com/gUEU7EuAjB https://t.co/zwPbXZSinX
The book is clearly out on undrafted tackle Kahlil Benson, but that can't be held against him too much considering he's being asked to fill a role he isn't suited for over this many games. Speaking of role, rookie wideout Cyrus Allen played a career-high 31 offensive snaps in Week 8 and had a couple of catches, including a big-time one on third down. The glaring red flag from his performance, unfortunately, was a missed connection on a deep ball he just didn't seem prepared for.
Defensive tackle Peter Woods, the second of Kansas City's two first-round picks, left Sunday's defeat to Denver with a neck injury. He's still flying under the radar overall, preventing him from going back to the upper tier of Chiefs youngsters. With Woods hurt, August waiver wire addition Bryson Eason was on the field for 20 defensive snaps (32.3% of those available) but didn't notch a tackle.
Once L'Jarius Sneed went to injured reserve, KC was immediately tasked with producing a slot replacement on defense. Fourth-round pick Jadon Canady wasn't a huge part of the solution, although his seven snaps played were significant nonetheless. The 23-year-old had a solid third-and-7 tackle on receiver Marvin Mims to open the second half and also closed on a play later in the third frame.
Wide receiver Jalen Royals' workload wasn't expected to increase with Rashee Rice back from a hamstring injury. Now that Allen is flashing some of his ability and the Chiefs are still rumored to be shopping for a wideout on the trade market, that'll only become more so the case.
For the first time since Week 1, former Clemson tight end Jake Briningstool converted on his lone target of the game and had a positive reception. That marked his second straight outing with just five offensive snaps.
Safety Xavier Nwankpa hasn't seen the field on defense since the last time the Chiefs won a game. Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa, who's made a nice special teams play or two for Dave Toub this year, still can't really crack the rotation for Steve Spagnuolo's unit.
As usual, nothing to see here. After being active but not registering a snap in Week 7, tackle Diego Pounds sat out this one. Quarterback Garrett Nussmeier assumed his weekly role as the emergency third signal-caller, with defensive end Jack Pyburn once again being organizational depth who won't play in games barring an injury to someone else.

title: Chiefs Stock Watch: Kansas City Failed Patrick Mahomes in Week 8 Defeat to Broncos
full_text:
Life comes at you quickly in the NFL, and the Kansas City Chiefs are perhaps the best example of that right now. In a matter of just two Sundays, the team's gone from riding high as an undefeated powerhouse to a club that's licking its wounds after suffering back-to-back losses.
Week 7's defeat at the hands of the Seattle Seahawks was a beatdown, but Week 8's shortcoming against the Denver Broncos raised the panic level even more. Despite some inspired performances from multiple players, others served as big enough culprits to drag everyone else down with them.
Let's dive into the good and bad from Week 8's Chiefs loss against Denver and single out three players whose stock is trending up, as well as three who could use a better showing in Week 9 and beyond.
These players stood out for positive reasons on Sunday, potentially changing the trajectory of their seasons in the process.
After going consecutive contests with no touchdown passes and an interception, quarterback Patrick Mahomes found himself on the wrong end of the post-Week 7 edition of this column. That came with a sentiment that he wouldn't be there for long, which wound up being the case thanks to his rebound effort on Sunday in the Mile High City.
Mahomes completed a staggering 30 of his 41 pass attempts for 321 yards and a trio of touchdowns, also going without a turnover for the first time in nearly a month. The two-time MVP was crisp, efficient and did a nice job of extending plays when needed. According to RBSDM , No. 15 was good for 0.24 EPA per play, and that might've been selling him short.
Kansas City let an improved Mahomes outing go to waste, which is a shame for everyone involved.
Entering Sunday's play, rookie running back Emmett Johnson had failed to receive a single rushing attempt in two of his previous three games. In the one contest he did get some work in, it was a three-tote, six-yard output against the Los Angeles Chargers. That left many to wonder whether the fifth-round pick would see an increased role at any point, only for the course to completely reverse on Sunday.
Johnson experienced by far his best game as a professional, and he did it in multiple ways. As a receiver, he made the most of his five targets by ripping off five catches for 128 yards and his first regular-season touchdown. He also broke off about as fun and hard-earned a 15-yard rush as you'll ever see. His work didn't stop there — he had a nice kickoff return on special teams, too.
The Nebraska product's blend of tough running, contact balance, smarts and improving pass protection make him closer to a starting-caliber player than someone who should be buried on the depth chart. Kansas City's completely revamped its halfback room in the best of ways.
Being a nose tackle in the pros is a pretty thankless job. Oftentimes, it's your name not being called that means you're fulfilling your role at a high level. Everyone knew that'd be primarily the case when Khyiris Tonga signed with the Chiefs earlier this year, but he's making a name for himself. After a six-tackle performance against Seattle, the 30-year-old picked up right where he left off.
Tonga finished with just two tackles in Week 8, but one was a run stop on halfback J.K. Dobbins that stood out on tape. He also batted a pass in the second half of play and, per Pro Football Focus , was credited with a pressure on quarterback Bo Nix. On an afternoon and evening that saw several members of the Chiefs fall short, Tonga Time was out in full force.
This group of three didn't meet the appropriate level of expectations in Week 8 and desperately needs to recover moving forward.
Another week, another instance of star center Creed Humphrey failing to do perhaps the simplest part of his complex job. How concerning is it that a four-time Pro Bowler and two-time All-Pro has been charged with a career-high six fumbles before the season is even halfway over? Humphrey acknowledged last week that he was working on resolving his problem, then he proceeded to fail again in a pressure-packed game.
Head coach Andy Reid spoke to the media on Monday and said Humphrey simply needs to "get the snaps up," yet it appears to be much easier said than done at this point. Until the former second-round pick strings together a few good showings in a row, it's hard to be confident that he'll put this confusing trend behind him.
When the Chiefs announced that L'Jarius Sneed was going on the injured reserve list and rookie Mansoor Delane would sit out Week 8 , they knew they'd be shorthanded at the cornerback spot. Not many folks doubted the ability of someone like Nohl Williams to get the job done on the outside or someone — anyone — to at least match Sneed's production in the slot, but the jury remained out on Kristian Fulton.
A whopping 60 snaps later, it's virtually impossible to feel much better about Fulton being a viable replacement for anything more than brief stints.
The veteran defensive back committed defensive pass interference on the Broncos' opening drive and later had an illegal block in the back on special teams. In the second quarter, he also totally whiffed on an attempted jam on wideout Courtland Sutton and got burned because of it.
Fulton remains someone who's a valuable depth piece and maybe even a trade chip , but don't confuse him for a starter on the same level of Williams or Delane.
Yes, we're cheating here and including a coach instead of a player. I think it's entirely justified, though, considering how much Reid melted down over the course of Sunday's contest. Penalties and on-field execution by the players were deserving of blame, sure, but Reid's baffling game management is still at or near the top of the list.
When the Chiefs opted to kick to try to go up 6 (never great!) our model had it as a toss-up between go...and punt. It saw field goal attempt as clearly the worst option. pic.twitter.com/Z7ugriKYkj
From botching a fourth-and-short to trotting out placekicker Harrison Butker for a boot he was bound to face an uphill battle to make, Reid fell flat against a bitter rival. He also still isn't explaining what's going on with benching left guard Kingsley Suamataia ; backup Mike Caliendo predictably struggled in relief.
Reid doesn't owe anyone answers, and his track record speaks for itself, but part of that includes decision-making concerns that crept back up at the worst time in Week 8. He needs to bounce back as badly as any of his players do.

title: The Good News and Bad News About the 2026 Kansas City Chiefs
full_text:
After back-to-back losses in the last two weeks , the Kansas City Chiefs are no longer the No. 1 seed in the AFC. They no longer hold the top spot in the AFC West . They've split with the Denver Broncos, meaning that the head-to-head tiebreaker they earned in Week 1 was one of many things wasted in their Week 8 meltdown.
Still, there is good news and bad news about where the Chiefs stand, particularly in the AFC. Do you want the good news first or the bad news?
The illusion of choice strikes again. It's all the same news.
Until further notice, the Chiefs are just another flawed contender in the AFC. How that makes you feel is a matter of perspective.
The AFC has somewhere between six and 10 teams that I could genuinely see making a playoff push that lands them in the AFC Championship Game. I could also see any of those teams being ousted in the wild card round. Sure, the Buffalo Bills seem like the worthy favorite, but who could be surprised by a mistake-filled opening-round loss to a barely-qualifying Houston Texans team that forces a few turnovers in January? No, I don't really believe in the Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) or Cleveland Browns (5-3), but at least one of those teams seems likely to be playing in the postseason, even if the Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) end up winning the AFC North.
Meanwhile, those heating-up Bengals just needed overtime to squeak past the lowly Tennessee Titans. Before that, they handled the Lamar Jackson-less Baltimore Ravens. Before that, they beat the then-winless Miami Dolphins by just seven points.
Look around the AFC and you'll see a wave of competent but unspectacular teams who do some things well and some things poorly. The good news is that the Chiefs still exist firmly within that class. The bad news is that they have been better than that for the majority of the Patrick Mahomes era.
The Chiefs, quarterbacked by Mahomes and with the AFC's only Super Bowl rings since Tom Brady's New England Patriots, are essentially neck-and-neck with Bo Nix's Broncos. Right there with the AFC North contenders who leave me uninspired. Tied in the standings with the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Bills are the only AFC squad with just one loss through eight weeks.
Kansas City isn't standing above their competition, reclaiming their boogeyman status for the rest of the AFC. They aren't sitting in the basement with other squads focusing on their 2027 NFL Draft boards. They're just sharing "flawed contender" status with the rest of the conference that has high hopes and measured expectations.
The Chiefs' path to the top should still be more climbable than others—Mahomes alone changes the math of what Kansas City can accomplish—but the Chiefs have enough flaws and have suffered enough self-inflicted wounds now that it's no longer reasonable to expect the best at every turn. Could they still represent the AFC in the Super Bowl? Absolutely. Could they be bounced weeks prior? Sure could. Just like everybody else.

title: Chiefs’ Need for a Wide Receiver Becomes Even More Glaring After Second Straight Loss
full_text:
After falling 28-24 to the Broncos yesterday, the Kansas City Chiefs suffered their second consecutive defeat and effectively lost their hold on the AFC West. Denver scored 15 unanswered points in the final quarter as the Chiefs' offense completely stalled out.
While the defense was largely responsible for the fourth-quarter collapse and Patrick Mahomes had one of his best statistical performances of the year, the issues with KC's offense became even more glaring . Andy Reid's squad had three opportunities to put points on the board in the final quarter and came up empty every time, including a two-minute drill where one more touchdown could have won the game.
Aside from Rashee Rice, who made his return from a hamstring injury, no Chiefs wideout surpassed 20 yards on the day. It was painfully evident down the stretch that Mahomes and his unit had no reliable options open downfield. This inevitably brought back doubts about the state of the wide receiving corps. During Monday morning's segment of Get Up on ESPN, NFL insider Adam Schefter resurfaced the idea that Kansas City has been actively searching for targets for Mahomes to throw to. He suggested it would be a surprise if a new face does not join the pass-catching group by next week's trade deadline.
"I think they are looking around for a wide receiver," Schefter said. "I think it would be a surprise if they didn't make some type of deal for some receiver before next Tuesday's trade deadline at 4 p.m. Eastern. They're going to look for a wide receiver, but that doesn't change that idea that this team needs better help up front and better play from its offensive tackle position."
“I think it would be a surprise if [the Chiefs] didn’t make some type of deal for some receiver before next Tuesday's trade deadline.” — @AdamSchefter on what he believes the Kansas City Chiefs will do heading into the trade deadline. pic.twitter.com/MopDZBiFru
Whether a move for a receiver comes later today or an hour before the deadline, general manager Brett Veach knows this is a primary point of concern for the Chiefs. It's only a matter of time before he pulls the trigger on a deal.
Even in a contest where the offense looked effective across three quarters, Kansas City's need for a receiver has become even more apparent. We've already explored a number of players they could look to acquire before the deadline, though the caliber of receiver they get depends on the draft capital they are willing to give up and the salary they are willing to take on.
Since losing Tyquan Thornton earlier this season to a dislocated ankle, the Chiefs' passing attack has often looked anemic. Thornton had unexpectedly emerged as perhaps Mahomes' favorite deep target, and his absence has been a significant blow. No matter how much we try to defend Xavier Worthy on a weekly basis, the reality is that he hasn't been living up to his billing as a WR2 . His route running has been anything but crisp, he struggles to make defenders miss in the open field, and his lack of size makes him a liability when he cannot utilize his speed in a straight line.
Internal options Cyrus Allen and Jalen Royals have flashed their talent at times, but it doesn't feel like they are ready to take on a prominent role just yet at this point in their careers. The outrage from Chiefs Kingdom if KC simply turned to its in-house prospects would be immense.
Going into this season, there were already lingering questions about the receiver group and how it would fare. Losing Thornton early in the year and seeing how the offense looked without Rice only magnified those concerns.
Schefter and many other reporters have confirmed the notion that Kansas City has been exploring the trade market. If the front office is truly committed to maximizing the championship window and giving Mahomes the weapons he needs, a trade needs to be made as soon as possible.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From Chiefs’ Week 8  Loss to the Broncos
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs lost a heartbreaker Sunday afternoon , and the race for the AFC West is officially on. The Denver Broncos took sole possession of first place after erasing an 11-point fourth-quarter deficit.
The Chiefs took the lead with just over six minutes left in the first quarter and held it until less than two minutes remained in the fourth. Kansas City then marched all the way down the field in an attempt to take it back, but a sack of Patrick Mahomes on fourth-and-goal from the Denver six as time expired ended all hope.
Here are the biggest winners and losers from the 5-2 Chiefs in Week 8.
The rookie was the Chiefs' runaway MVP in this game, filling the stat sheet in several different ways. Emmett Johnson led Kansas City in receiving with five catches for 128 yards, including a 73-yard touchdown that gave the Chiefs a 14-6 lead.
He carried the ball just once for 15 yards, but forced four missed tackles on that play alone, according to PFF. As a fifth-round pick from the 2026 NFL Draft, he is also a core special teams player, and he made his presence felt there, too.
The former Nebraska Cornhusker recorded a tackle in kick coverage on the very next play after his touchdown and returned a kick 44 yards to set up the Chiefs’ final comeback attempt. On a day when the next-highest pass catcher had 67 yards and Kenneth Walker ran for just 69, Johnson’s impact was enormous.
Patrick Mahomes was not always perfect, but when you throw for over 300 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions, it is a good day at the office. He made do with what he had, and what he has is well documented.
He continues to play behind an undrafted backup left tackle, with Josh Simmons on IR. Left guard Kingsley Suamataia was once again benched in what was labeled a coach’s decision, and the wide receiver room leaves much to be desired.
Rashee Rice returning gave him some easy yards, but the rest of the group did little. Cyrus Allen continued to earn trust, ranking third among receivers in snaps behind Rice and Xavier Worthy and catching two passes for 20 yards, both for first downs. Worthy, the receivers’ snap leader, caught three of six targets for just 13 yards.
Mahomes’ wide receivers combined for only 90 of his 308 yards, with Rice accounting for 53 of them. He gave the team a chance right up until the end, when he took his second sack of the game.
George Karlaftis has been a mainstay in the winners column, and Sunday was no different. The stat that stood out most was three batted passes, some of which ended or stalled Denver’s drives.
He sacked Bo Nix in the second quarter on what was actually a strip-sack, though Denver was able to fall on the ball. He is now the only Chiefs defender with multiple sacks this season.
These numbers can vary greatly, pending final review, but PFF counted just five pressures for defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s unit. It wasn't nearly good enough, especially in the fourth quarter, but Karlaftis continued to show why general manager Brett Veach extended the 25-year-old.
The Chiefs had all the momentum heading into the fourth quarter. The defense had forced three straight three-and-outs in the third, and Mahomes had just thrown his third touchdown to make it 24-13. The next two offensive drives cost them the game, and head coach Andy Reid made two decisions worth second-guessing.
The first came at the top of the fourth quarter, when he punted on a fourth-and-less-than-one from his own 41. Given how well the defense was playing, that was forgivable, though succeeding on such short yardage could have put the Broncos out of their misery.
The second was more questionable. On the next drive, facing fourth-and-eight from the Denver 36, Reid sent out a struggling Harrison Butker , who missed from 54 yards. Even a made kick would have put Kansas City up six, and the Broncos scored seven shortly after, so the point is not that Butker missed the kick.
J.J. Watt noted on the broadcast that the analytics say to punt there, which would have forced Denver to drive the length of the field while down 24-21. The other option was to go for it and continue an 11-play drive that had chewed up more than six minutes. Instead, the Chiefs walked away with nothing, and Denver got tremendous field position on the drive that led to the go-ahead touchdown.
Right tackle Jaylon Moore, who missed last week’s loss to the Seahawks with a concussion, did not have the most glaringly bad game, but he made the worst mistake of any Chiefs lineman.
Mahomes and the offense got the ball back down four with 1:56 left and marched to the Denver one-yard line with ease. On fourth-and-goal, Mahomes found Rice for what looked like a walk-off touchdown against their biggest rival.
The play was blown dead before it started, however, because of subtle pre-snap movement from Moore, resulting in a false start. To make matters worse, Moore allowed quick pressure from Denver defensive end Jonathan Cooper on the game-ending play, ending Week 8 in the most dramatic and worst way possible.
For three quarters, the defense played about as well as you could ask. The only thing that hindered it was costly penalties that extended drives and led to Denver’s first 13 points. Penalties plagued the Chiefs all afternoon, and the Chiefs were flagged 11 times for 105 yards, with 63 of them on defense alone.
Then came the fourth quarter. Denver gained 121 yards and scored 15 unanswered points, and on the two game-deciding drives, the Chiefs allowed a 10-yard run, a 22-yard pass, a 14-yard run, and a 51-yard pass. The Broncos entered the day near the bottom of the league in both yards and points, and while the Chiefs looked close to shutting them down as they did in Week 1, they still allowed 28 points in a critical divisional loss.

title: Chiefs HC Andy Reid Remains Silent on Kingsley Suamataia’s Second Benching in Four Games
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' downward spiral continued on Sunday evening with a heartbreaking 28-24 loss to the Denver Broncos . Even after leading by double digits halfway through the final quarter, Andy Reid's squad let the game slip away and squandered its grip on the AFC West lead.
Amid the ongoing controversy with the franchise stemming from the questionable signing of Justin Tucker to the practice squad, the off-field issues only grew today with another troubling development. For the second time in KC's past four contests, head coach Andy Reid made a puzzling decision to bench a key starter in the trenches. During pregame warm-ups, Mike Caliendo was seen taking first-team reps over Kingsley Suamataia. It was strikingly similar to the Chiefs' Week 4 matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders back in October when the third-year lineman was benched for the veteran backup. Indeed, Suamataia's absence in the defeat was once again a "coaching decision."
The last time this happened, Reid remained tight-lipped on the situation and made it clear that the details would remain private. When he was asked about Caliendo taking over at left guard in his postgame press conference today, his answer was the same.
"Yeah, that's just between Kingsley and I, so," Reid briefly responded.
The Chiefs have confirmed it's a "coach's decision" on Kingsley Suamataia. Mike Caliendo set to start at left guard. https://t.co/WoU0UqMFBh
Prior to his first trip to the bench before Week 4, Suamataia had taken every snap at left guard in 2026 and played exceptionally well. Since then, it feels like a coin toss determining who is going to occupy the position every week.
Both instances were likely disciplinary or accountability-driven decisions by the coaching staff. ESPN insider Nate Taylor revealed that Caliendo was privately named the starter the day before kickoff against the Raiders, confirming that Reid and his staff made a premeditated choice. The consequences came into focus when Caliendo was overpowered by Malcolm Roach and surrendered what ended up being a walk-off sack for Denver on the final play from scrimmage, which certainly didn't sit well with the fanbase.
Andy Reid benched his starting LG for unknown reasons again. Watch the backup LG on the final play of the game. pic.twitter.com/Uo5DxTq2Xp
Superstar tight end Travis Kelce weighed in on the matter postgame as well, noting that he isn't aware of what led to Suamataia's benching but said he trusts the coaching staff's judgment.
"He's family. Everybody has their own road," Kelce told the media. "We love Kingsley, we think he's a hell of a player. At this time, I'm not even sure what the scenario is. I'm rolling with whoever we've got in that game. I'm sure Kingsley is drooling, trying to get back out there." The uncertainty surrounding the move is only compounded by the fact that Suamataia is not dealing with an injury . Fans have been left in the dark with his status since he is not included on injury reports leading into games.
While the coaching staff isn't sounding the alarm over this two-game losing skid, things are starting to unravel in Kansas City. Constantly sitting one of your top linemen for undisclosed reasons is not exactly a way to turn things around.

title: Andy Reid Is Embracing a Simplified Approach After Chiefs' Complicated Loss to Broncos
full_text:
Despite controlling Sunday's Week 8 outing against the Denver Broncos for most of the afternoon, the Kansas City Chiefs couldn't get out of their own way. That trend only worsened into the early evening, culminating with a brutal loss on the road.
The 28-24 defeat brings Kansas City to 5-2 through seven games, also putting it behind its rivals in the AFC West standings for the first time all season. It's a loss that should hurt for a variety of reasons, especially with it being the result of numerous issues.
As he always does, though, head coach Andy Reid is taking the even-keeled route. Speaking to the media following Sunday's game, he emphasized the need to quickly turn the page and focus on what's ahead.
"Listen, things happen," Reid said. "There are a few more games left. We've got to make sure we rally from this, learn from it and then move on. That becomes important."
Reid singled out missed tackles and penalties as two things that Kansas City would benefit from cleaning up. At the same time, he alluded to his club still being right in the thick of it at the end, even after a compounding effect of mishaps set in.
"They made some plays there," Reid said. "I mentioned the tackling, we could've made some tackles. We were in position to do that; you've got to make those. Just like the other part of it is the penalties. You're playing a good football team, so when you do these things, you're not going to normally come out on the right end of it. We were in position to win the game, the penalty happened and we don't get the touchdown."
One can essentially take their pick of the litter when it comes to responsibility for this game's outcome. At a fundamental level, going on the road to Mile High and taking on a club that made the AFC title game earlier this calendar year is a challenge in and of itself. Finding a way to win when you commit 11 penalties for 105 yards and have a trio of three-and-outs further amplifies that.
Washing all of that down with a missed field goal, multiple poor fourth-down calls from the head coach and a defensive collapse at precisely the wrong time spells out doom. That's exactly what the Chiefs got, as they went from seemingly en route to a statement victory to getting punched in the mouth and having no suitable response.
The Broncos’ win probability fell to 10.2% early in the fourth quarter and was just 11.9% with 2:44 left in regulation in their comeback win over the Chiefs. Denver’s chances of winning the AFC West are now 64%. With a loss, they would have been 24%. Powered by @awscloud pic.twitter.com/yTc9UFmuQx
That's the kicker, though: Kansas City was remarkably close to still getting out of Dodge with a plus in the win column in the face of so many self-constructed roadblocks. It presents the team with a strange reality, as it showed several potential red flags while simultaneously lending credence to his unwavering belief that things will be corrected.
Reid actively served as a part of the problem in Week 8. His decision to punt on a short fourth down at his own 41-yard line was brought into question, as was his third-and-2 play call on the following drive that resulted in a sack on quarterback Patrick Mahomes (and a missed field goal by the struggling Harrison Butker ).
The offense, for yet another week, struggled to produce points under late-game pressure. The dam of the defense finally broke after Butker's miss. The special teams unit, obviously, was anything but special. Reid, tasked with putting his men in the best positions to succeed, didn't do that at the most important stages of the contest.
This doesn't have to become a lingering set of circumstances, but pressing the reset button immediately is paramount. It's one thing to say it and another to do it, although Reid's been on both sides of that coin.
Following a complicated loss, that's the simplicity of his message.
"I've got a good locker room," Reid said. "I know we work the right way here. We have to learn from it — that's what you do — and you move on. Work on the next one, which is a good Jets team coming in. We'll be ready to go."

title: 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs' Heartbreaking Week 8 Loss to Broncos
full_text:
Coming off their first loss of the season, the Kansas City Chiefs appeared to make a concerted effort to put forth a more inspiring performance. They managed to do so for most of Sunday against the Denver Broncos, although it wasn't in a winning effort.
Head coach Andy Reid's crew seemed to be in control for a good chunk of Week 8, only to fall short down the stretch and suffer a crushing defeat to a bitter rival.
With the 28-24 loss, the Chiefs fall to 5-2 on the year. Let's jump into 10 instant observations and takeaways from Week 8.
Blocking isn't the most head-turning element of the game, particularly for a skill-position player, but it should be discussed more. Especially for a team that operates in 12-personnel (one running back, two tight ends) with frequency, it's an important part of an offense. Travis Kelce, at age 37, being far and away the superior blocker between him and Noah Gray is an issue.
Gray's poor blocking chops showed up giaringly in the first half on two occasions — once in the run game and once in pass protection. Some of his shortcomings could be chalked up to a smaller and lighter frame , but his angles and leverage are oftentimes poor as well. This is a nitpick for someone who otherwise made an impact on Sunday, but it's long overdue to be mentioned.
Kansas City simultaneously flashed a much-improved offense over Week 7's production while also having a variety of rough moments that reminded everyone of why there's a long way to go. On one hand, quarterback Patrick Mahomes had a staggering 195 passing yards and two touchdowns. On the flip side, the Chiefs averaged only 3.5 yards per rush attempt and only kept the ball on the ground eight times.
Add in a 1-for-5 conversion clip on third down and there being three-and-outs on three separate occasions, and you get a more complete picture. This is a group that still needs to establish more consistency in play-calling decisions, execution, timing and more, but the first half of Week 8 was a step in the right direction. Not even a few dead drives in half No. 1 can take away from that.
Ending up with double-digit penalties for triple-digit yardage is inexcusable. Sure, one ticky-tacky holding call on right guard Trey Smith made up part of that total, but that doesn't explain the rest of the bunch from Sunday.
Some infractions were more procedural in nature, such as a false start on Kelce, an illegal formation charged to left tackle Kahlil Benson and an ineligible man downfield flag on right tackle Jaylon Moore. Others, though, were worse and simply cannot be repeated. Linebacker Jack Cochrane and safety Alohi Gilman each had unnecessary roughness penalties in Week 8, making life harder than necessary for the defense.
Some special teams issues and a rough outing for cornerback Kristian Fulton didn't help matters one bit. Moore's false start on a fourth-and-goal at the end of the game was the not-so-sweet icing on the cake.
Last week, I wrote a bit about defensive end Ashton Gillotte as someone whose stock is on the rise . Truthfully, it's easy to forget that he sustained a plantar fascia injury during training camp and started the 2026-27 campaign at a slow pace. He's ramped that up in a big way in recent weeks, however, and this game was no different.
Gillotte had a good run stop on Denver's opening drive, made a quality read on its second possession and also chipped in on a double-effort run stop in the second quarter that wasn't credited in the box score. The sophomore man continues to prove that he's a starting-caliber player, which is great for the Kansas City defensive line.
One thing that All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones made a name for himself for early in his career was tipping passes at the line of scrimmage. When defensive end George Karlaftis entered the league in 2022, his water polo background was brought up on broadcasts seemingly every week. That history continues to pay off years later, evidenced by two pass breakups in the second frame on Sunday.
Rookie pass rusher R Mason Thomas also had a batted pass on the Broncos' third drive. Defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga notched one in the third quarter to help cap off his solid day at the office. This is clearly something defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo and defensive line coach Joe Cullen emphasize, which pays off.
For weeks, plenty of folks who follow the Chiefs (this writer included) have wondered when rookie running back Emmett Johnson 's breakout would occur. It was only a matter of time before he found a way to make an impact, and he had a multitude of signature moments over the course of Sunday afternoon and evening to make his presence known in a huge way.
Starting with the supporting elements of his game, the Nebraska product had an amazing 15-yard run that looked reminiscent of many from starter Kenneth Walker III. On special teams, he had a 44-yard kickoff return late in the fourth quarter that helped put the offense in a great starting position. It was Johnson's output in the receiving game, though, that made a huge difference.
The first-year man was excellent out of the backfield, taking a beautiful pass from Mahomes to the house for 73 yards and also adding a 38-yarder near halftime. In the fourth frame, he recorded a third-and-2 reception to move the chains as well. If there was ever a week for Johnson to establish himself as a viable option down the stretch, it was this one.
THE ROOKIE EMMETT JOHNSON WITH A 73-YARD TD KCvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/sGCPC0rJYU
Rookie wideout Cyrus Allen got some more run in this one and even had a nice eight-yard reception on an out route in the third quarter. A clutch third-and-12 snag also provided a glimpse of the possible chain-moving, reliable threat he can become if he realizes his potential.
With that said, the Cincinnati alum seemed to slow up early on a deep pass from Mahomes. Perhaps Allen just didn't think the ball was coming his way and was too late to realize it was, but it was a rough look either way. A play like that could've given him a totally different stat line and earned him some good graces with Mahomes and the coaching staff, so it's undoubtedly a missed opportunity.
When the Chiefs brought in kicker Justin Tucker on the practice squad this week, it sent a clear message that starter Harrison Butker was on thin ice with the organization. Reid shot down high-level concerns regarding the longtime franchise favorite following Week 7's loss, but it might be time to push the conversation forward even more.
Sure, some rain made Butker's 54-yard field goal in the fourth quarter more difficult, but he's paid handsomely to make these kicks under pressure. That miss swung momentum to Denver's favor and things quickly devolved from there, so part of this loss falls squarely on the veteran placekicker's shoulders. His seat has to be warming up even more.
There's plenty of blame to go around in this one. The aforementioned penalties were a killer at various points in the contest, and Reid did himself and his team very few favors with how he managed the fourth quarter.

You can lump in the defense's poor — and rapidly poor — response to the Butker miss into the pile, too. For a team that's led by vets both on the paying surface and on the sideline, this one stings. It's easily one of the more prominent and obvious collapses of the Reid-Mahomes era.
Don't get it twisted: Kansas City isn't doomed in the division race by any stretch of the imagination. That said, failing to maintain the head-to-head tiebreaker over a hot Broncos team is suboptimal. Rising to 4-0 in the AFC West and creating more padding to kick off the month of November would've been massive for a team that's now floundering just a bit.

title: 3 NFL Trade Deadline Deals the Chargers Should Explore Right Now
full_text:
Now that the Los Angeles Chargers are 0-7 and still the only winless team in the league, it is important to look into the upcoming NFL trade deadline and see what the options are for the team and its future.
The trade deadline is Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. ET, so making these decisions as soon as possible will be crucial for general manager Joe Hortiz. What are some plausible moves he should explore?
The number one name in Chargers media in regard to trades is the veteran EDGE defender, Khalil Mack. The argument for trading him away is simple: He is an aging veteran who is playing well and deserves to be competing at this stage of his career.
The Chargers are 0-7 and about to be mathematically eliminated from the NFL postseason. Allowing Mack to compete is only fair. The only bump in the road is that the Chargers will be relying on rookie first-round pick Akheem Mesidor to be their full-time starter. He has played well enough to earn the spot.
Head coach Jim Harbaugh has also come out and said that he wants Mack on the team. So the question is: does Harbaugh's desire for Mack to stay outweigh the value of trading the veteran defender?
#Chargers HC Jim Harbaugh on whether Khalil Mack will be given a chance to go to a contender if he wants to: “I want Khalil Mack here. Khalil Mack wants to be here. He’s one of the pillars of our team.” pic.twitter.com/k728dLXoNv
Estimated Trade Value: 2027 Fourth-Round Selection
JuJu Brents is a former second-round selection of the Indianapolis Colts in 2023, being known for his man-cover skills and impeccable size and speed. Standing at 6'3, Brents had some ups and downs with the Colts, eventually moving on to the Dolphins, where he has been solid for a team that is also at the bottom of most NFL power rankings.
The Chargers could in the market for a cornerback with Derwin James Jr. being placed on injured reserve and their cornerback room needing depth outside of Cam Hart, Tarheeb Still and Donte Jackson (who could be a trade candidate in his own right). It should be noted that in the one start from practice squad CB, Isas Waxter , he looked like he could play at the NFL level.
If the Bolts bring in Brents, it would allow for a deeper room with much more upside going into 2027. That is all the team should be looking for if they were to go out and trade for someone.

Dalvin Tomlinson is another veteran on this Chargers defense who deserves to play for a team that is in actual contention. While Tomlinson has been hurt, he showed flashes early in the year, showing that he still has what it takes to compete.
If Tomlinson is healthy and a contending team needs just a bit more run-stuffing ability, he could be the perfect buy-low candidate for any team in that situation. The Chargers should get what they can out of a guy who was supposed to be a one-year rental, anyway.

title: Chargers' Criminally Overlooked Trade Candidate's Departure Would Fix Some Issues
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have an interesting big board of trade targets at the deadline , considering they’re the worst team in the NFL, clutch the No. 1 pick in the draft order and need to think beyond this season.
That also means the Chargers are positioned as big sellers at the trade deadline. Khalil Mack is the obvious name to go first , if Jim Harbaugh and the club actually change their stance on trading away players.
But there are some overlooked Chargers players who could be on the move, too. Think, veteran cornerback Donte Jackson, should a contending team get really desperate at the premium position.
But there’s another sleeper name worth considering: Kimani Vidal.
Sure, running back isn’t a premium spot anymore. But its importance has been upped in recent years again, hence the Chargers going after Omarion Hampton in the first round at all.
Speaking of the Chargers and Hampton, Vidal is a pretty sneaky trade candidate because we can’t help but mention that offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel is effectively ruining him.
No exaggeration: Hampton has effectively managed to regress from his oft-injured rookie season. He’s carried the ball just 89 times for 309 yards and three scores on a 3.5 average. McDaniel has often preferred to yank him from the lineup in favor of Keaton Mitchell (39 carries, 15 catches) and Vidal (29 carries, nine catches).
Hampton is supposed to be the workhorse first-round product. The other guys are role players. That’s why Harbaugh is getting questions about, well, not splitting up the touches in the backfield so much.
“Yeah, maybe,” Harbaugh told The Athletic’s Noah Furtado . “I think that’s something that we’re looking at, and I think we’ll try that, yeah. … I’ve been in that position before (with a three-back rotation), and it’s worked. I also think there’s a place to getting the backs in rhythm.”
Vidal, a sixth-rounder in 2024, has been a really fun success story through the way he has played well when given a chance amid injuries on the depth chart. He’s a solid way for other contenders to beef up their rotations before the playoffs.
Granted, a Vidal trade wouldn’t get much back in return. But for the Chargers, removing one overthinking roadblock for McDaniel and getting Hampton back on track might just be worth more than any late-round pick they get for Vidal’s departure.
