title: Raiders Release Telling Injury Report Ahead of 49ers Matchup
full_text:
After snapping their four-game losing streak against some of the league's best teams by beating the New York Jets in Week 8, the Las Vegas Raiders returned to the practice field on Wednesday. Sunday against the Jets, the Raiders rallied in the second half to pull away from a red-hot Jets offense and team.
The Raiders used every second on the clock to secure their first victory in weeks. They also blended what had worked well in their three-game winning streak with adjustments ahead of and during their Week 8 road matchup against the Jets.
Win or lose, Klint Kubiak and his coaching staff have kept things even-keeled within the locker room.  The Raiders look to start yet another streak with another road win this Sunday.
Las Vegas will be on the road again in Week 9 when they face the San Francisco 49ers. Week 9 reminds us that Las Vegas has one of the league's toughest schedules, yet they have already surpassed last season's win total. At 4-4, the Raiders are still ahead of schedule.
It is early, but not too early to note that even at .500, the Raiders are technically still in the playoff hunt halfway through the season. Under Kubiak, Las Vegas has beaten the teams they have improved enough to beat. This is, again, more than can be said about recent Raiders teams.
Still, the Raiders committed to excellence long ago. They hired Kubiak to help them recommit. That will require the Raiders to continue what they have been doing and more. After the work Las Vegas' front office put in this offseason, it is okay to hold that standard.
The four teams the Raiders have beaten this season have a 5-24 record. For the Raiders to get where they want to go, they will have to beat at least a team or two with a winning record.
What better week than this week against a talented San Francisco team?
For Las Vegas, the next step is to take the things they have done in their four wins against the four teams they have beaten and do those things against the league's best, which the Raiders will continue to face over the next few weeks. Las Vegas has to, and can, steal a game.
If the Atlanta Falcons can beat the 49ers, the Raiders can, too. Anything is possible on any given Sunday. However, Las Vegas will have to quickly improve on both sides of the ball before Sunday to have a realistic chance of pulling off what would be their biggest win of the season.
This Sunday, Las Vegas will have another chance to beat a team that they shouldn't beat when they head West to face the San Francisco 49ers. The Raiders took the practice field on Wednesday to prepare for a 49ers team that started the season 6-0.
San Francisco poses several issues for Las Vegas on both sides of the ball. Las Vegas will have their work cut out for them. This is especially true for the Raiders' defensive backfield, which has had a long few weeks. The unit has had its expected struggles, and some unexpected ones.
This Sunday could be an even tougher task for the unit, depending on starting cornerback Darien Porter's status. The second-year cornerback missed practice on Wednesday with a groin injury that forced him to miss all but one play against the Jets in Week 8.
Darien Porter, Jackson Powers-Johnson, and Patrick Johnson did not practice on Wednesday. Brock Bowers, Quay Walker, Kwity Paye, and Jack Bech were listed as full participants. Folorunso Fatukasi, DJ Glaze, and Ian Thomas were listed as limited participants on the report.
The Raiders released receiver Cody White on Wednesday and activated tight end Carter Runyon from Injured Reserve. Runyon fully participated in Wednesday's practice.
In addition to Porter, Las Vegas also listed on Wednesday's injury report.
Las Vegas' coaching staff has been cautious, doing what they can throughout the week to ensure their best players are as healthy as possible. It will be interesting to see how the rest of the Raiders' week of practice turns out in terms of the roster's health.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Analyzing Raiders CB Stokes' Game-Changing Impact Amid Clear Struggles
full_text:
There is no way around it. Wide receiver Adonai Mitchell is underrated, but Las Vegas Raiders cornerback Eric Stokes had a bad outing against the New York Jets on Sunday. Geno Smith and the Jets went at Stokes and the Raiders' defensive backfield early and often with a high success rate.
Entering the offseason, the Raiders' defensive backfield was the team's biggest question mark. After a productive season with Las Vegas last season, Stokes re-signed with the team, cementing himself as the team's top option at the position. That has remained the case throughout the season.
However, Sunday was arguably the worst game Stokes has had since joining the Raiders. Darien Porter's injury after the first play of the game and Las Vegas' need to stop the run forced defensive coordinator Rob Leonard to lean on his veteran and the rest of the backfield in man coverage.
This left Stokes on an island with several young, quick, and agile wide receivers and a quarterback with the arm to deliver the ball accurately and on time. It made for a long day for Stokes and the rest of the backfield. It also confirmed what was already largely suspected.
Stokes' solid 2025 season saw teams throwing away from his side of the field, as he usually made plays that made it not worth trying. Yet, as the team's best cornerback, if teams broke through Stokes' coverage, it would look a lot like it did against the Jets.
It was not pretty, but Stokes battled the entire game. Even with the Jets racking up catches and yards, mainly on him, Stokes continued to push through. Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak shared his thoughts on the veteran cornerback.
“No, I think [Eric] Stokes also made some really big plays for us. He had a tough assignment. They made some plays on him, but he also made some really big plays for us, especially in the red zone. He’s been a great competitor for us. But as the competition continues and young guys make plays, we’re going to play the best guys," Kubiak said earlier this week when asked if he and the coaching staff had any talks about potentially replacing Stokes on Sunday.
The fact of the matter is, no matter how bad Stokes plays, he is the best cornerback the team has. As bad as he played on Sunday, he did not give up many big plays, despite the fact that the Jets went at him a significant number of times.
“I think the Jets had a really good plan overall, and I think again, when you play defensive back in the NFL, yeah, you’re going to get beat. At some point you’re going to get beat, but how do you respond when that happens? And when a defensive back gets beat, everybody knows about it,” Kubiak said.
“If a guard loses in the run game, it’s not discussed as much. So, you’ve got to have thick skin. You’ve got to be able to move on to the next down, and so I’m really glad we have number five [Eric Stokes]."
Despite his struggles, Stokes had two plays on the Jets' first two scoring drives that helped Las Vegas' defense force field goals instead of touchdowns. Stokes broke up two passes in the end zone, one on third down.
This cost the Jets eight points. Las Vegas won by five. It was not pretty. Stokes must fix things quickly, with a tough few weeks ahead, but considering the Raiders held the Jets to 26 rushing yards in the second half while leaving Stokes on an island, something worked.
Through it all, Stokes continued to battle, refusing to let a disappointing outing deter him. Stokes and the Raiders' defensive backfield deserve the spotlight that comes with a subpar performance. However, they also deserve the spotlight for the game-changing plays they made on Sunday.
Las Vegas' defense has struggled to stop opponents' ground and passing game this season. Sunday against the Jets, the Raiders decided to eliminate the run, which cost them through the air.
The Raiders have had a questionable defensive backfield for multiple seasons. Sunday's defensive backfield performance shouldn't surprise anyone who has followed the unit over the past few seasons. This has been building for years.
That said, if Stokes has another game as he did against the Jets, I would be curious how healthy he is and whether he's potentially been quietly working through a health issue.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Film Room: The Decisions That Changed Week 8
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders traveled to the East Coast to face a New York Jets team that was quietly better than their record indicated. The Raiders quickly learned this, as New York rushed for 140 yards in the first half and held the Raiders' offense to 97 total yards.
The Raiders needed every second they could get to pull out a win over the Jets. Below are the biggest decisions Klint Kubiak and his coaching staff made that impacted Sunday's win.
The Raiders were faced with a tough decision down the stretch. Las Vegas could have punted the ball back to the Jets up by two points with little time left on the clock. Or the Raiders could kick a field goal from midfield to go up by five.
Missing the field goal would have given the Jets the ball back near midfield against the Raiders' struggling defense, needing only a field goal to win. With the game on the line, Las Vegas trusted their kicker, Matt Gay, who has only missed one field goal this season.
Gay has been one of the most dependable players on the roster this season. Las Vegas' special teams accounted for 14 of the team's 38 points on Sunday.
Las Vegas needed more from their ground game in various ways. Starting Washington sparked the Raiders' offense in more ways than one. However, his success on the ground was not only because of him; the Raiders made other changes that helped the ground game get going as well.
As we mentioned following Las Vegas' loss to the Los Angeles Rams in Week 7, not playing Zuhn more, specifically at a position of need, was becoming a more curious decision by the week. The Raiders drafted Zuhn because of his ability to play all five positions along the offensive line.
However, with three out of the five starting positions on the line solidified and their struggles at offensive guard, the Raiders finally gave the rookie a try at a position that had been derailing the entire unit. Overall, Zuhn did well in his first start at offensive guard.
This is even more notable because he spent most of his productive collegiate career at offensive tackle. Zuhn also confirmed during the offseason, entering his first offseason in the league, that offensive tackle was the position he is most comfortable with.
Still, Las Vegas has had a revolving door at offensive guard this offseason. It was clear that neither Jackson Powers-Johnson nor Caleb Rogers was able to play the position at a high enough level long enough to help Las Vegas' offense get going. The opposite may be true about Zuhn.
Mike Washington Jr. — Week 8 carries vs NYJ (All-22, EZ angle). 25 carries total. Part 1/3 🧵 #Raiders pic.twitter.com/MCfW05OxVR
The Jets are the Jets. Zuhn's performance at the position moving forward will be worth keeping an eye on. In one game at the position, he looked more qualified for the position than anyone else the Raiders have tried this season. Furthermore, they have tried their best options at the position.
At this point, it is Zuhn or bust. If Las Vegas cannot get a solid remainder of the season from Zuhn at guard, there is little more they can do to fix the position. Week 7 gave reason to be cautiously optimistic about Zuhn's immediate future at the position.
Dependable play from their offensive guards is one thing the offense has lacked this season. If Zuhn becomes another starting offensive lineman for the Raiders as a rookie and plays well, that gives John Spytek and the Raiders' front office plenty to consider ahead of the trade deadline.
Zuhn becoming a starter halfway through his rookie season at a position Las Vegas wasn't going to address until the offseason would keep them ahead of schedule and make for another successful pick for Spytek.
It would add even more value to the trade that landed Zuhn and rookie safety Treydan Stukes. The San Francisco 49ers will be a much stiffer test for Zuhn and the Raiders, but at the very least, he is no worse than any of the other players the Raiders have tried at right guard this season.
At the very most, he may be their starting right guard for the forseeable future.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Game Review: How Key Rookies Performed vs. Jets
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are back in the win column and sit at .500 after eight weeks. The win against the New York Jets was a breath of fresh air for a Raiders team needing to end a four-game winless skid that left them winless in October.
The Raiders tried a few new strategies that garnered some encouraging results, including a change at running back and right guard, while more of the younger defensive backs saw their number called and played significant snaps.
I spent some time rewatching the game from Sunday and focusing specifically on the five rookies who saw increased snaps. Let’s take a look at my notes from the Raiders' win against the Jets.
When Darien Porter went down on the first play of the game, in came rookie cornerbacks Hezekiah Masses and Jermod McCoy , both of whom played at least 25 snaps.
Masses flashed this week with a much more consistent day in coverage and made arguably the biggest defensive play of the game outside of Jeremy Chinn’s game-winning interception. On a third-and-long inside the Raiders' 15-yard line with less than five minutes to play, Masses baited Geno Smith working the flat-corner Cover 2 side of Cover 6. He worked into the flat, then sank with depth to the corner and made an excellent play on the ball to force a field goal.
McCoy saw the most snaps of his career so far and was what you would expect from a talented defender still working his way toward feeling comfortable with his previously surgically repaired knee. McCoy was inconsistent, with a toolkit that saw him change direction with a snap but misplayed his technique in certain coverages, such as trail or man-to-man.
Safety Treydan Stukes had a much better day than he had in the last month. I thought he did well to close on the football in both the run and passing game, using his short-area burst to close the distance. He made a nice pass breakup on Kenyon Sadiq early in the game while showcasing the ability to cover a lot of ground as a single-high defender, so this game was an encouraging moment for Stukes.
I think the Raiders found their mainstay at right guard for the time being. Trey Zuhn III made his first career start and looked as good as I thought he would.
As a run blocker, I thought Zuhn had sufficient drive and push at the point of attack, showcasing good climbs to the second level with ease thanks to ample functional athleticism for the position. He did a great job torquing his hips to seal off stretch plays and played with good short-area quickness to reach his landmarks.
Zuhn has to do a better job hitting his landmarks with better timing and could’ve gotten off duo or combo blocks to hit the second-level defender, though sometimes it was the Jets linebackers scraping over the top at a lightning-quick clip.
In pass protection, the athleticism is clear when the former third-round pick was mirroring and matching pass rushers from the interior, displaying good mobility. There were times when Zuhn’s lack of length hurt him against long-levered defenders, but he made up for it with good timing and hand strikes in his sets, matching that with an improved anchor from his college days. I found myself encouraged by Zuhn’s performance.
With 25 carries for 83 yards, the rookie from Arkansas was impressive as the lead tailback , with Ashton Jeanty working out of a role as the third-down pass-catcher out of the backfield.
Washington is getting more comfortable fitting into head coach Klint Kubiak’s wide zone-blocking scheme. Kubiak did well to mix up his gap and zone-blocking concepts to get the best of both worlds for Washington.
The fourth-round selection from this past spring played with sufficient vision and followed his blockers well, and he has a large, powerful frame for a running back that allows him to handle a workhorse load. I thought Washington could’ve attacked backside cutback opportunities, and that will come with more reps and feel at this level, but he was a handful to bring down in space.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Why Week 9 Should Determine Raiders’ Decisions For 2026
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders sit at 4-4 after defeating the New York Jets in Week 8.
If the Raiders had lost that game , which would have been a fifth consecutive defeat, the front office's hands would have been forced at the trade deadline. However, the win puts Las Vegas somewhat in limbo in that regard, as you could make an argument either way about whether the team should look to sell off pieces before Nov. 10.
Obviously, head coach Klint Kubiak and these players want to compete and challenge for a playoff spot. Unfortunately, the Raiders are in ninth place in the AFC playoff picture. The Chiefs, Bengals, Patriots, and Browns are the four teams currently occupying or competing for the wildcard spots.
In Week 9, the Raiders travel to Santa Clara to take on the San Francisco 49ers, who are 6-1 and coming off a bye. We'll go through each scenario - win and loss - and determine what Las Vegas should do at the trade deadline based on those results. Disclaimer: This game takes place on Nov. 8.
Facing a Kyle Shanahan-led team coming off a bye week is a daunting situation for the Raiders. Nevertheless, Las Vegas leaving Week 9 with a win two days before the trade deadline would make it a fascinating 48 hours for the front office.
In a world where the Raiders pull off the upset, the only position they should pursue in the trade market is a wide receiver. Now, the timing of all this complicates matters, as players such as Brian Thomas Jr., Josh Downs, and George Pickens could all either be moved elsewhere or stay with their current teams. If none of those players are available, Las Vegas likely ends up staying pat.
Even if Las Vegas wins, I would still consider moving Maxx Crosby and maximizing his value, with teams clamoring for a premier pass rusher.
It's quite simple: with a defeat, the Raiders should be open to trading away multiple key veterans, including Crosby and Kirk Cousins . That doesn't mean Las Vegas should give these players away for less than their value. If the right offer doesn't come to the table, the Raiders shouldn't force a trade.
Why I feel so strongly that general manager John Spytek should open the phone lines if the Raiders lose is that they face the Seahawks, Broncos, and Browns in the ensuing weeks. The probability of exiting that stretch above .500 - especially with a Week 9 loss - is slim to none. Get out ahead and get as much value for aging, productive players who don't fit Fernando Mendoza's timeline .
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Dolphins Tuesday Mailbag: How Should We Evaluate the Rookie Class?
full_text:
Part 1 of the post-Patriots game Miami Dolphins on SI mailbag:
Why hasn’t any reporter asked either the head coach or the special teams coach what is up with the kickoff/punt coverage? Or maybe they have and I’ve missed it. But can’t we do better than simply just kicking out of the end zone and giving up the 35-yard line? Thank you!
Hey Rob, yes, Jeff Hafley and Chris Tabor have been asked and you make a valid point because ideally you’d like to pin the opponent inside, say, their own 25 and that can happen easily with a penalty on the return, for example. The flip side, though, is giving the ball at the 35 with the touchback eliminates the possibility of a big return, and there’s value in that as well. Another factor is the idea of providing the special teams game reps in kickoff coverage, which is not happening with the touchbacks. So, yeah, maybe covering kickoffs again might be the play here.
Was it due to the lousy weather conditions against the Pats, or are we going to continue to see a short game passing attack by the Dolphins?
Hey Ed, the Dolphins utilized a short passing game against the Jets and it worked great. Against New England, there were a couple of shots downfield, including the late touchdown pass to Kevin Coleman Jr. I don’t think we want as many shots downfield as we saw in the early weeks and the New England was good in that sense. There just has to be better execution along with better production from the run game.
Hi Alain, from your perspective in the locker room, how are team morale and confidence changing each week as the losses accrue? Is it noticeably different to what you have seen since the 2019 season?
Hey Matt, it’s all about expectations and the make-up of the team, and in 2019 as in 2026 it’s mostly a young group that fully understood the challenges ahead. Nobody likes losing and there’s always frustration after a loss, but we haven’t seen any effect on team morale or confidence to this point, and I suspect we won’t at any time during the season.
From Jorge Francisco boyd:
Hi Alain, with the way we played against the Patriots, do the Dolphins have any chance to win against Detroit and, if so, why? Is Chop Robinson coming into his own?
Hey Jorge, last question first, and the answer depends what you mean by “coming into his own.” If you’re asking whether Robinson has improved from last year, then the answer is yes. If the question is whether Robinson has arrived as an impact player, the answer is there’s still more to be done, and it starts with consistency. Robinson has been a major topic of discussion lately because his pass-rushing metrics are really, really good, except that some (like me) just don’t see that on film and we also have to remember he’s pretty much a pass rusher still at this time. As for the Detroit game, sure, the Dolphins can win, but I suspect it would take a gigantic effort from the offense because I don’t see how the defense will slow down the Lions.
I know it’s early, but what do you see as the positions of need for next year’s draft?
Hey Charles, it might be quicker to point out the positions where there’s no need. But I’d say the ones that stand out, assuming the main players are back in 2027, would be edge defender, cornerback, tight end, safety, defensive tackle and guard. Quarterback comes into the picture if the Dolphins decide that Malik Willis simply isn’t the answer and I personally am not ready to do that.
I’m a big fan of both of our 3rd round WRs. I’m waiting for the Chris Bell awakening. When is it coming? Also, shoulder issue? Omar hinted at something on the collective. Appreciate the answer and your work!
Not aware of a Chris Bell shoulder issue, so can’t speak to that, though we’ll get an injury report Wednesday and might see if there’s something there. I’ve been saying for a bit that I think it’ll be toward later in the season, if not next year, that we see a Bell awakening, as you call it. As this time, he looks like a solid possession receiver and nothing more, but I think there’s more to his game.
Alain, I know there is a lot of hype on the Dolphins rookie draft class; I’m optimistic as well. Is this class possibly overrated because so many get to play as rookies? If on veteran teams many would only play special teams, opportunities abound this season. Thoughts?
Hey Jeff, can’t disagree with anything you said there. I also think that every time a rookie makes one play, it seems to be portrayed later on as having had a great game, even with some breakdowns later on. As you said, there’s every reason to be optimistic about what the Dolphins have in their 2026 draft class, but I think we would do well to wait a bit before we start anointing too many players based on highlight plays here and there.
Alain Poupart is the publisher/editor of Miami Dolphins On SI, host of the All Dolphins Podcast, and co-host of the Dolphins Collective. Alain has covered the Miami Dolphins on a full-time basis since 1989 for various publications and media outlets, including Dolphin Digest, The Associated Press and the Dolphins team website. In addition to being a credentialed member of the Miami Dolphins press corps, Alain has covered three Super Bowls (for NFL.com, Football News and the Montreal Gazette), the annual NFL draft, the Senior Bowl, and the NFL Scouting Combine. During his almost 40 years in journalism, which began at the now-defunct Miami News, Alain has covered practically every sport at one time or another, from tennis to golf, baseball, basketball and everything in between. The career also included time as a copy editor, including work on several books, such as "Still Perfect," an inside look at the Miami Dolphins' 1972 perfect season. A native of Montreal, Canada, whose first language is French, Alain grew up a huge hockey fan but soon developed a love for all sports, including NFL football. He has lived in South Florida since the 1980s.

title: Dolphins Week 8 Report Card: Front Seven Earns Highest Marks
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins have gone right back to leaving one on the table.
Miami led New England 13-3 at halftime at Hard Rock Stadium before giving up 21 unanswered points in a 24-19 loss.
There were encouraging individual performances, particularly from some of the Dolphins expected to eventually beome foundational pieces.
But there were also penalties, stalled possessions and coverage breakdowns
Malik Willis finished 21-of-32 for 211 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. He didn’t offer much as a runner this time, rushing for just 2 yards on one carry.
He looked encouraging in the first half while completing 12 of 15 passes for 112 yards and helped Miami finish the half with a touchdown after zipping a pass to Malik Washington in the goal line.
The second half wasn’t as smooth however, with 73 of his 99 second-half passing yards coming on the final touchdown drive.
His interception came after an unfortunate ricochet off a defensive lineman’s helmet, but he threw another one that was erased by an offside penalty. The passing game needed more consistency before the deficit reached 11.
The next step in Willis’ development may require a few more uncomfortable seconds in the pocket. Offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik’s slower-developing play-action concepts, particularly those sending only two receivers downfield, require patience. The defensive backs need to show their hand, and at times that means open routes won’t show up until the last second.
Ollie Gordon II finished with 69 yards on 19 carries, averaging 3.6 yards per attempt. Jaylen Wright added 5 yards on two carries, and Miami managed just 74 rushing yards overall.
Bobby Slowik keeps trying to find small ways to change the picture for opposing defenses, like offsetting Gordon farther to the right in the backfield instead of just stacking him behind the quarterback. This time, his creativity wasn't rewarded.
The bigger problem was Gordon’s third-quarter unsportsmanlike conduct penalty, which turned a manageable third-and-5 into third-and-20. Miami punted, and Gordon’s frustration spilled onto the sideline.
Willis later said he told Gordon he was “dead ass wrong.”
Kevin Coleman Jr. continues developing and showcasing the route-running ability that can make him a reliable fixture in the receiver rotation
On his 35-yard touchdown, Coleman sold the out before turning upfield, giving Charles Woods a taste of the turf.
He caught all three of his targets for 46 yards and a touchdown.
Malik Washington continues to produce at a steady clip, with Miami putting his skills to use near the goal line on a short motion that created a matchup against safety Kevin Byard III, and Washington stopped on a dime before sprinting to the flats and catching a 1-yard touchdown.
Washington finished with five catches for 40 yards. Caleb Douglas added four for 43, while Chris Bell caught four for 31.
Greg Dulcich followed his season-high performance against the Jets with four catches for 43 yards.
His 19-yard reception on third-and-8 helped keep Miami’s touchdown drive alive before halftime.
The blocking looked rough, though.
New England kept generating pressure through matchups against Miami’s tight ends, primarily Will Kacmarek, who had difficulty holding up against Gabe Jacas and Elijah Ponder, most notably on a failed cutblock midway through the first quarter.
The first two sacks weren’t necessarily examples of terrible blocking. They were longer-developing plays where nobody was open before somebody eventually got free.
Jonah Savaiinaea, however, had a couple of reps that didn’t require much explaining.
With 7:45 left in the first quarter, he reached with his hands, leaned too far forward and absolutely whiffed as Christian Barmore knocked his punch away. Barmore and Gabe Jacas finished the sack.
At 5:05, Savaiinaea was driven backward by Cory Durden, who helped blow up Gordon’s run for a 3-yard loss. Savaiinaea also committed a holding penalty before halftime.
Miami was without Kadyn Proctor, with Jarrett Kingston starting at left guard. Still, five first-half sacks and 74 rushing yards make it difficult to be generous with this grade
Josh Uche has pretty much defined serviceable this season.
He might not be keeping offensive tackles awake at night, but he generally does his job.
On a misdirection run, much of the defense followed Corey Kiner’s jet motion. Uche stayed home and was able to corral Rhamondre Stevenson. He also finished with four tackles and a third-down sack that dropped Maye for a 10-yard loss.
Chop Robinson added two sacks and showed some versatility beyond rushing the passer. On third-and-5 with 9:22 left in the first quarter, he bluffed a rush before dropping into the middle of the field, helping take away an option as Maye threw incomplete.
Robinson also had a chance to bring Maye down before DeMario Douglas’ 48-yard touchdown and couldn’t finish it.
The tackle totals are impressive, but watching Jordyn Brooks and Jacob Rodriguez help each other is becoming almost an art form.
One will step up and stonewall a blocker to clear space for the other. They’re willing to do the dirty work even when somebody else gets to finish the play.
Brooks finished with 11 tackles, while Rodriguez added eight and punched the ball out of Efton Chism III’s hands. JuJu Brents recovered, giving Miami the short field that produced its first field goal.
Willie Gay Jr. continues to live a life of extremes, and this time it ended badly. He bit on Drake Maye’s fake pitch near the goal line, allowing the quarterback to keep it for the go-ahead touchdown.
Michael Taaffe is naturally the type of player you want to root for. A former walk-on, willing tackler, always ready to throw himself into somebody.
But, man, he keeps getting beaten in coverage.
Kyle Williams jetted across his face on the deep post for a 43-yard touchdown. New England used motion to create that matchup within Miami’s Cover 3, and Williams said afterward that he knew it would be a touchdown when the play was called.
At this point, it’s worth wondering how much Miami can hide those weaknesses by walking Taaffe closer to the line and giving him more work against the run.
JuJu Brents also gave up Douglas’ 48-yard touchdown. Maye finished 16-of-20 for 199 yards and two passing touchdowns, completing 9 of 10 for 146 yards after halftime.
Wright continues to do more damage returning kicks than carrying the ball on offense
He returned five kickoffs for 142 yards, including gains of 43 and 36 yards. He did, however, failed to make the simple play of stepping out of bounds while fielding a kickoff near the sideline in the fourth quarter, which would have resulted in a New England penalty and Miami getting the ball at its 40. Instead, there was a holding penalty on the play and Miami began that drive at its 12.
Zane Gonzalez connected from 31 and 52 yards, but missed a 43-yard attempt with 6:41 remaining that would have cut Miami’s deficit to eight.
Bradley Pinion averaged 45.8 yards on four punts, with a 37.0-yard net, while Miami allowed Marcus Jones a 26-yard punt return.
There was some improvement in the return game, but another missed opportunity when Miami needed points.
Miami built a 13-3 halftime lead, then went right back to getting in its own way.
This team plays hard for Jeff Hafley, and while it may sound like a consolation prize, it should be the most encouraging sign of this entire process so far.
Tyler M. Carmona is a Miami native whose work has appeared in the Miami Herald and Associated Press. He previously worked as a local television news reporter. He recently graduated from Columbia University’s Graduate School of Journalism and played college football at Savannah State University and the University of St. Francis

title: Examining the Mistakes that Cost the Dolphins in Week 8 ... And How to Fix Them
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins gave themselves a chance to pull off an upset against the New England Patriots in Week 8, but ultimately came up short at Hard Rock Stadium.
Maybe the simplest explanation is that New England is a better team that rose to the occasion in the second half when the Dolphins failed to do so, with a dubious replay overturn clearly not helping matters, but Miami also did it to itself.
As young teams are prone to doing, the Dolphins hurt themselves with mistakes that had little to do with the Patriots.
They are the type of mistakes the team will have to eliminate to continue the progress they've already shown in the early stages of this massive rebuilding project.
This is the one that stands out as the biggest self-inflicted wound because it was so unnecessary, and it turned a third-and-5 situation into a third-and-20 on the Dolphins' second drive of the third quarter after New England had scored to cut their lead to 13-3.
The Dolphins needed to at least get a first down or two to stop the Patriots momentum, but Gordon gave them no shot.
Gordon got an earful from quarterback Malik Willis on the sideline after the drive after head coach Jeff Hafley also talked to him, but beyond Gordon having to hear it from his teammates, this is one mistake with no easy fix beyond Gordon learning how to control his emotions.
And that's the tricky part, right? Because we want Dolphins players to play hard and with passion, but also control their emotions once they reach a certain point.
The fix here isn't benching Gordon because he's become so important to the offense with De'Von Achane on injured reserve.
Of course, if this happens a couple more times this season, then there'll be a major problem, but for now let's just hope he's learned his lesson.
Look, missed field goals happen, it's just that Zane Gonzalez badly going wide left on a 43-yard attempt down 24-13 midway through the fourth quarter basically sealed the Dolphins' fate.
It's not like the Dolphins are operating with a great margin for error, so they basically need their kicker to be near-perfect — like Riley Patterson was in 2025 when he went 27-for-29.
Gonzalez missing (again, badly) on his third attempt during his second practice squad elevation should make the Dolphins think long and hard about devoting a roster spot to him after he's elevated for a third time next Sunday against Detroit.
Sure, Drake Maye deserves maybe a small degree of credit for shaking off Johnson's tackle attempt when he came in free from the blind side on a fourth-down blitz, but that was way more about Johnson and what he did wrong.
The day after the game, why Johnson dove at Maye's legs instead of running through his back remains a mystery. Even more so because Johnson has been a good tackler — maybe ever a great tackler for a cornerback — so far in his rookie season.
Maybe he got too excited about the possibility of a big play, maybe he was going too fast and lost some body control. Regardless, this is a teaching moment for the Dolphins' defensive coaches because, again, it's not like Johnson isn't physical or a good tackler.
The Dolphins should have started their drive after New England took the lead at 17-13 at their own 40, but instead began at their 12 after Jaylen Wright fielded the kickoff near the sideline and Julius Wood was flagged for holding.
All Wright had to do was put himself out of bounds before touching the ball — it wasn't difficult — and that would have resulted in a penalty on the Patriots.
Yes, that drive ended with the Malik Willis interception off the helmet of a Patriots defensive lineman, but the yardage difference off the kickoff based on the same sequence of events would have given them the ball after the pick at their own 19-yard line instead of their 47. Maybe they call plays differently from back there and don't score the touchdown that made it 24-13.
In any event, this should be Kick Returning 101 and we've seen player after player in the NFL do that move and invariably earn praise from TV analysts for their great awareness.
Here's the thing, though: This is something special teams coordinator Chris Tabor already should have drilled into every one of his kickoff returners, whether it be Wright, Malik Washington or anybody else who's gotten practice reps back there.
And now he should remind his returners before every kickoff about the rule.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 8 Loss
full_text:
Some things are too good to be true, including the Miami Dolphins winning two games in a row, as they fall to New England by a painfully close score of 24-19.
To many fans, the idea of "tanking" and not messing up their draft stock went out the window as soon as they saw that a win over the Patriots was possible, and it certainly looked that way at halftime. However, the offense, defense, and special teams all seemed to regress in the second half.
In the end, the Dolphins lost their third straight game by a touchdown or less. A competitive game for sure against the defending AFC champions, but it's the Patriots. Any loss against them is guaranteed to sting.
To see Savaiinaea on this list is frustrating because this performance came out of nowhere. He's been having a stellar resurgence for the Dolphins this season, but if everyone is guaranteed at least one stinker per season, this was certainly it for him.
The first half was especially difficult for Savaiinaea. Mainly matched up against Christian Barmore and Corey Durden, he struggled to give Malik Willis time in the pocket and was a non-factor in blocking for Ollie Gordon and Miami's run game.
Barmore breezed by Savaiinaea for a sack on Willis on their second drive of the game on third down, forcing a punt despite being near midfield. And while it didn't end up mattering because Miami scored four plays later, he was called for a holding penalty that wiped a 15-yard touchdown for Gordon off the board.
This performance by Savaiinaea really came out of left field. He hadn't allowed a sack or committed a penalty through the first seven weeks of the season. The o-line obviously took a hit with Kadyn Proctor not playing, but the Dolphins will hope this was a one-time slip-up and nothing more.
The jokes about Robinson appearing on milk cartons should thankfully be over after his performance against the Patriots. After the shaky start to the season he had, he's only gotten better, and he blew up against the Patriots with three solo tackles and two sacks.
In the first half, the Dolphins sent the house on Drake Maye play after play, usually to resounding success. His second sack came after getting past a trio of New England linemen, literally brute-forcing his way to the quarterback and forcing a punt.
That said, New England eventually cracked the code in the second half, and Miami's pass rush began to sputter. But for Chop specifically, this was the game he needed to start proving to Miami that he deserves to stay a member of the Dolphins. Consistency is key, however, and it won't get any easier against Jared Goff and Detroit's offense.
OK, there's really not much that Johnson did wrong in this game. He actually provided much-needed durability to the secondary, being one of four players to play all 60 defensive snaps alongside Jacob Rodriguez, Jordyn Brooks and Michael Taaffe.
Really, there's only one major thing he did wrong, but he likely won't hear the end of it for a while. On fourth-and-2 with five minutes to go in the second quarter, Johnson had Maye dead to rights, breezing by Eli Raridon and facing the back of Maye, who never saw him coming. It looked like a surefire sack.
Instead, Johnson dove low and to the left of Maye, who then completed a 12-yard pass to extend the drive. Thankfully for Johnson, New England would go on to miss an ensuing field goal, but it's an awful look for the rookie. If he's given 100 chances to tackle Maye in the same situation, he would likely take him down 99 times, but unfortunately not 100.
How do you, as an underdog, wish to upset a team that has aspirations of making it back to the Super Bowl? You need a spark, and Rodriguez delivered that in the second drive of the game.
Down by three, Rodriguez performed his signature peanut punch on Efton Chism III, knocking the ball free. It was ultimately recovered by JuJu Brents and led to the Dolphins tying the game with a field goal of their own. That fumble proved to both Miami and New England that the Dolphins' defense could hang with the Patriots.
The list of winners and losers for Week 8 is filled with players who earned their spots mainly based on a single play. But every play matters more in a game that was won or lost by seven points or less.
That said, this was a disappointing game for Gordon, who was held to 69 yards on 19 carries. Is it too surprising? Not really, as the Patriots have one of the best run defenses in the NFL. As we mentioned earlier, his best run of the day was wiped off the board due to a holding penalty.
But in Miami's second drive out of halftime, Gordon committed an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty that resulted in a third-and-20. Not surprisingly, it forced a Dolphins punt, and the Patriots drove 73 yards in 13 plays to score a touchdown and take their first lead since early in the first quarter.
Gordon was irate on the sidelines, having to be cooled down by his quarterback. His emotions have been tested multiple times this season, including their loss to Cincinnati, but at least that tantrum was limited to the sidelines and, to some, justified given their struggles. But costing the team 15 yards and indirectly leading to a Patriots' lead that they wouldn't give up is unacceptable in a game like this.
Coleman was only targeted three times in this game, but he was a guaranteed target in all three of them, recording 46 yards. However, his final reception is an early highlight for the fifth-round pick.
It's not just that he scored a 35-yard touchdown that gave the Dolphins a sliver of hope with just about two minutes to go. It was the way he did it, absolutely shredding Charles Woods' ankles. His draft profile, which highlighted his speed and effectiveness after the catch, checks out.
Between Coleman, Douglas, and Bell, the group of rookies contributed almost equally in this game in terms of receptions and yards. It's a nice sight to see, but if anyone had doubts about what Coleman can contribute from the trio, he shut them down with that touchdown.
Miami's offense looked promising in the first half, taking a 13-3 lead to the break. But everything unraveled for the unit after halftime, and the play-calling on offense was a major contributor.
Even looking away from the back-to-back punts in the third quarter, the tempo of the offense in the fourth was off. They were at a deficit but handled the situation like they were ahead, draining 10 minutes and 23 seconds off the clock in their final three drives. Had they picked up the pace, there may not have been a need to go for an onside kick after the Coleman touchdown.
It didn't feel like there was a sense of urgency you would expect for an offense down by double digits with not much time remaining.
Pinion was asked to punt four times in this game - an unfortunate number, but he was at least consistent - with his kicks going 50, 40, 45, and 48 yards, respectively. His best work was his second attempt, pinning the Patriots deep at their 15-yard line.
Was it anything too special? Not really, but factoring in the not-so-optimal weather conditions and how sloppy the field can get, it was refreshing to see a mistake-free game for him. Pinion also handled a pair of kickoffs, resulting in a touchback on both occasions.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 8 Snap Counts Stories: Rookie Revelations, Top Guys Emerge
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 24-19 loss against the New England Patriots on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by guard Kadyn Proctor missing the game because of a concussion.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Kyle McCord and offensive lineman Andrew Meyer.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to six rookies with Proctor being out. The six starters were fullback DJ Herman, Will Kacmarek at tight end, wide receiver Caleb Douglas, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- There two things that stand out about the offensive snap counts, both of them involving rookies.
-- While Malik Washington missed a few plays after taking a big hit to the head on a play that resulted in a personal foul flag against New England, Caleb Douglas still looked like he emerged as the No. 1 wide receiver in this game. He played 56 of the 65 offensive snaps, compared to 48 for Washington and Chris Bell also got an elevated role with 45 snaps. That was a big jump from Bell's 31 snaps against the New York Jets in Week 7.
-- Then there was rookie tight end Will Kacmarek, who played only 20 snaps on offense, his lowest total since the season opener after he had dealt with injury issues in training camp. Kacmarek has been on the injury report in recent weeks with a hamstring problem, and if that's the reason his snap count was limited, then maybe the Dolphins need to sit him for a game to get him completely healed. If not, we'd question using him so little when the running game could have used extra blocking help against the Patriots.
-- Kacmarek's usage on offense ended up being the same as Herman, and we just don't understand that — again, barring injury complications.
-- It again was the Ollie Gordon II show at running back, as he played 53 snaps (82 percent) and Jaylen Wright got only eight offensive snaps. Given Wright's lack of production — he's averaging 1.9 yards per rushing attempt this season — it's difficult to argue against the snap distribution here, though the Dolphins might eventually want to take a look at recent waiver wire pick-up Kaytron Allen.
-- Veteran Jalen Tolbert was active but got only six offensive snaps, by far the fewest of any of the wide receivers.
-- Four players were on the field for all the team's 60 defensive snaps — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe and CB Chris Johnson. Those were the same four with 100 percent participation against the Jets in Week 7.
-- Josh Uche again led all edge defenders with 48 snaps, with Chop Robinson second with 33. Rookie seventh-round pick Max Llewellyn got only two defensive snaps and didn't play on special teams, and one can't help but wonder why the Dolphins wasted his third and final practice squad elevation for that amount of work. The Dolphins now won't be able to use in another game this season unless they sign him to the 53-man roster.
-- Also note that Llewellyn's low snap count happened even though fellow edge Malik Herring missed some game time because of an injury before returning.
-- The Dolphins went big on about a third of their defensive snaps with at least three of their interior defensive linemen. The snap counts behind Zach Sieler were pretty even between Jordan Phillips, Zeek Biggers and Kenneth Grant, with all of them getting between 27 and 37 snaps.
-- In his second game back after being on IR with a knee injury, rookie Kyle Louis played a season-high 11 snaps on defense in a nickel role.
-- Linebacker Willie Gay Jr., back after missing the Jets game because of illness, played 27 defensive snaps alongside Rodriguez and Brooks.
-- Tackle Chukwuebuka Godrick, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers from the Kansas City Chiefs after the cuts to 53, made his season debut and it consisted of four snaps on special teams.
-- Godrick and Kaytron Allen were among the six non-specialists who saw action only on special teams, along with LB Shaka Heyward, LB Jackson Woodard, CB Reese Taylor and G/T Caedan Wallace.
-- Finally with special teams, rookie Seydou Traore again led the way with 22 snaps, followed by 17 for Julius Wood, followed by 16 each for Louis, Heyward, Woodard and Allen.

title: Miami Dolphins Week 8 Instant Takeaways: Second-Half Collapse Costs Potential Signature Win
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins really had a shot at getting their first signature win of the Jeff Hafley era, they really did.
But if it hadn't already been established, the game served as a reminder this is a team that's operating with a very small margin for error, and there were a few too many of those in the second half, along with a controversial officiating reversal that changed the momentum.
Truth to be told, this was an encouraging performance by the Dolphins in the big picture, even if they did let one slip away after leading 13-3 at halftime after completely shutting down an injury-riddled New England offense.
The Dolphins are making progress, that's what's important here. And, yes, they did make progress and still look much improved from the team they were in the early weeks of the regular season.
Dolphins fans no doubt will lament the replay official overturning the Dolphins' fourth-down stop when they were leading 13-10 in the third quarter, instead giving New England a first down that kept alive what became the touchdown drive that gave them the lead for good.
But it wasn't the only play that swung the tide.
Ollie Gordon II got flagged for an unnecessary and, frankly, stupid unsportsmanlike conduct for yapping at an opponent to turn a third-and-5 into a third-and-20 in that forgettable third quarter. Then Zane Gonzalez, elevated from the practice squad for a second consecutive week, badly missed a 43-yard field goal attempt to basically put the Dolphins in a position where there only shot was to recover an onside kick, which basically never happens in the NFL anymore.
Beyond that, New England simply was the better team in the second half when they outscored the Dolphins 21-6, though the Dolphins again were plucky and fought to the end, as we figure they'll do all season even if the wins aren't that frequent.
-- It figured that Gordon would have a tougher time against the Patriots, particularly with Kadyn Proctor missing the game with his concussion, and that's how it played out. And we wouldn't fret over his ability to have other big games.
-- While we don't necessarily complain about play-calling, there was a pretty obvious lack of urgency in the fourth quarter when the Dolphins were down two scores and still running the ball, and often letting the play clock run down.
-- This isn't their identity, but this was a game where the Dolphins needed to air it out in the fourth quarter, not be calling running plays on second-and-12.
-- Malik Willis was fine, even though his performance wasn't as good as it was against the New York Jets. He certainly wasn't the reason the Dolphins lost.
-- Guard Jonah Savaiinaea has no doubt made significant improvement in his second season, but there's still some lapses that show up in his game.
-- Jarrett Kingston did a respectable job in place of rookie Kadyn Proctor, though he had to overcome a shaky start.
-- On the flip side, Austin Jackson had one of his best performances of the season.
-- The defense hardly could have played better in the first half and it seemed as though everybody chipped in.
-- What hurt more than anything in the second half were the two big plays, the two long touchdown passes that accounted for almost half of Drake Maye's passing yardage.
-- Props to Jacob Rodriguez for creating a turnover with a perfect Peanut punch, though he overall had a pretty quiet game.
-- The pass defense continues to get shredded, with Maye completing 80 percent of his passes. The coverage on DeMario Douglas' 43-yard touchdown was particularly depressing as he caught a pass wide open between defenders and had so much space that he could zigzag the rest of the way to the end zone.
-- Chris Johnson is normally a very good tackler, which is why it was so baffling to see whatever that was that he attempted against Maye when he came in free from behind for what should have been a sack. He should have had redemption later on that drive with a fourth-down stop, but of course there came the overrule from the replay assistant when television replays didn't suggest anything obvious enough to overturn the original ruling.
-- That play was just yet another example why instant replay stinks.
-- Yes, Willie Gay Jr. looked kind of bad on Maye's rushing touchdown off an option play, but the reality is he was one defender against two offensive players. There didn't appear to be anybody outside to handle the pitch had he zeroed in on Maye, so he was kind of in an impossible position there.
-- The special teams again had a rough outing, but missed field goals will happen and long punt returns allowed unfortunately have become commonplace. What's unforgivable is Jaylen Wright fielding a kickoff near the sideline instead of putting himself out of bounds before touching the ball, which would have created a penalty on the Patriots and given Miami the ball at its 40. Those are fundamentals the Dolphins simply have to recognize.
-- Guess we could blame it, like everything else, on Miami being a young team. But those are the kind of mistakes we want to see disappear sooner rather than later.
-- In the final analysis, though, this was a frustrating loss because the Dolphins put themselves in position for the big upset and weren't able to deliver. The first part alone, though, was a sign of progress.

title: Examining the Outside Factors That Could Impact the Dolphins' Week 8 Game Against New England
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' Week 8 matchup against the New England Patriots won't be lacking for storylines, including Miami's quest for a second consecutive victory, but there are some that go beyond X's and O's.
The Dolphins will go into the game following their breakthrough 28-25 victory against the New York Jets to face the defending AFC champion Patriots, who have a 4-3 record following a Thursday night loss against the Chicago Bears in Week 7.
The Patriots will go into the game missing star wide receiver A.J. Brown and backup running back TreVeyon Henderson, while the Dolphins will be without rookie first-round pick Kadyn Proctor with star running back De'Von Achane on injured reserve.
New England will enter the game as a 7.5-point favorite, according to the FanDuel Sportsbook, but if you believe in the idea that weather can be an equalizing factor, then the weather in Miami Gardens on Sunday should be considered.
It was raining in Miami Gardens on Sunday night, but the forecast called for the weather to actually get worse — if not much worse — throughout the afternoon and into the night.
The outlook as of 10 a.m., according to Weather.com, read as follows: "Storms likely for the next several hours. Potential for heavy rainfall."
There also is a flood watch in several areas of the northern parts of Dade County, where Miami Gardens is located.
With the expectations of thunderstorms, we also can't help but look back to the Dolphins' 2018 season opener against the Tennessee Titans when two lightning delays lasting more than an hour each made the game last more than seven hours.
And obviously the field conditions could become a factor at some point with the ball getting slippery and footing also potentially becoming an issue.
The other outside factor in the Dolphins-Patriots game that needs to be watched, even though it hopefully won't affect the outcome one way or the other, was the officiating crew switch late in the week.
The officiating around the NFL has come under a lot of scrutiny this season, but it may have reached a high point (or low point maybe?) in the Green Bay Packers game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field last week, leading to Packers safety Xavier McKinney lashing out publicly after the game.
McKinney drew a fine from the NFL for using the term for bovine excrement in talking about the officiating, but he wasn't the only one complaining.
Ton Brady openly criticized at least one call for roughing the passer during the game, but the most egregious call came for an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty when Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown got up after catching a pass, a Packers defender tackled him thinking the play wasn't over but knocked down an official in the process, with the official responding by throwing a flag while on his back.
Likely as the result of not wanting the spotlight on the officiating crew of Alex Moore, the NFL took them off their scheduled assignment for the Sunday night game between Philadelphia and Washington and moved them to the Dolphins-Patriots game, which will be shown to a ridiculously small portion of the country as the "other" 4:25 p.m. on CBS opposite Kansas City at Denver.
Moore's crew, for the record, officiated the Dolphins' home opener against the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 3, calling eight penalties on each team. Moore also worked the Dolphins-Patriots game at Hard Rock Stadium in Week 2 of 2025.

title: Breaking Down the Dolphins Saturday Updates, but More Importantly What Went On with New England
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins made their customary practice squad elevations Saturday, including that should precipitate an upcoming move, but it was what went on with the England Patriots that really was newsworthy.
For the second consecutive week, the Dolphins elevated both kicker Zane Gonzalez and edge defender Max Llewellyn.
Gonzalez was a given considering the Dolphins don't have a kicker on the 53-man roster and it was his second such promotion. After one more elevation, the Dolphins then will have to sign him to the active roster and find themselves a new kicker. And for those wondering, there's no financial or cap incentive to just elevate kickers from the practice squad because that move entails the elevated player getting the prorated active roster salary for that week, along with the accompanying cap hit.
Llewellyn, for his part, actually will be out of practice squad elevations after this week because along with the Week 7 game against the New York Jets, he also was elevated in Week 2 for the game against the San Francisco 49ers.
Llewellyn could put himself in line for a permanent promotion with a strong outing against the Patriots on Sunday. The Dolphins already had five healthy edge defenders for the New England game with Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Malik Herring, Rodney McGraw and newcomer Jamree Kromah, but the latter just joined the team late in the week and it's almost a given to be inactive.
The big news with the Patriots came earlier Saturday afternoon when the team announced that both wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back TreVeyon Henderson had been downgraded to out after both being listed as questionable Friday.
To replace them, the Patriots signed running back Lan Larison from their practice squad to their 53-man roster and elevated wide receiver Ryan Miller from their practice squad. Yes, that's the same Ryan Miller who played four games for the Dolphins this season and has the team's longest offensive play of 2026 with his 77-yard touchdown reception from Malik Willis toward the end of the Week 2 loss against the San Francisco 49ers.
Brown and Henderson being out is big news for the New England offense, which already has wide receivers Romeo Doubs and former Dolphins player Mack Hollins on injured reserve. With those two out, the biggest threats for the Miami defense, besides obviously QB Drake Maye, will be running back Rhamondre Stevenson and tight end Hunter Henry.
New England's top three wide receivers for Sunday will be Kyle Williams, Efton Chism III and DeMario Douglas. Corey Kiner will become the second running back option after Stevenson.

title: The Chris Grier Firing One Year Later: Revisiting the Former Dolphins GM's Hits and Misses
full_text:
Halloween arrived Saturday, but for the Miami Dolphins it also marked the one-year anniversary of the firing of Chris Grier as general manager, a move that was met with almost universal approval from the team's frustrated fans.
His eventual replacement, Jon-Eric Sullivan, has on the flip side won over a lot of folks with his early moves in a massive rebuilding project that was almost necessary because of previous mistakes by his predecessors and the other decision-makers in the organization.
While Sullivan's draft class has the looks at this time of a slam-dunk winner with the early contributions of Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, Caleb Douglas and Michael Taaffe, though it probably will take some time to offer an accurate verdict, and the same goes for the most involving the veterans (though, again, the Jaylen Waddle trade looks a winner at this time).
Grier's firing came on the morning of October 31, 2025, hours after the Dolphins dropped a 28-6 Thursday night decision against the Baltimore Ravens at Hard Rock Stadium.
Sullivan was hired as GM in January after Champ Kelly finished out the 2025 season as interim GM, making one trade during his time.
That was the move to send Jaelan Phillips to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for a third-round pick, a decision that was sound at the time and even more so now after the huge contract Phillips got in the offseason from the Carolina Panthers as an unrestricted free agent.
Grier had taken over that role in 2016 after more than a decade with the organization, though in many ways he assumed true GM duties in 2019 after the Dolphins moved on from Executive Vice President of Football Operations Mike Tannenbaum.
The Dolphins failed to win a playoff game during Grier's time as GM, extending a drought that began in Grier's first year with the team in 2000.
Along the way, Grier oversaw a series of personnel decisions that did lead the Dolphins to the playoffs three times, including his first year in 2016, but also came up way short considering all the financial commitments the Dolphins made.
In breaking down the Dolphins' personnel decisions, we should point out that the organization always went out of its way to talk about a collaborative approach but as GM the hits and misses should fall on Grier more than anybody else.
And, without question, it's in the draft where Grier had most of his misses.
-- The Dolphins whiffed on too many early draft picks over the past decade, a trend that started with first-round pick Charles Harris in 2017 and continued with Noah Igbinoghene in 2020, Liam Eichenberg in 2021, Channing Tindall in 2022 and Cam Smith in 2023.
-- The Dolphins also missed out on some big-time talent, which happens to every franchise but seemed to happen more often for Miami. Just last year, the Dolphins took Kenneth Grant at number 13, one spot before the Colts took Tyler Warren, and that decision still doesn't look very good 18 months after the fact. But while the final verdict isn't in on that dubious choice, here's a long list of more clear regrettable choices:
• DE Charles Harris over T.J. Watt in 2017 Round 1 • QB Tua Tagovailoa over Justin Herbert in 2020 Round 1 (yes, even though Herbert is struggling badly with former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel as his new offensive coordinator this year) • T Austin Jackson over WR Justin Jefferson in 2020 Round 1 • CB Noah Igbinoghene over RB Jonathan Taylor or S Antoine Winfield in 2020 Round 1 • OL Liam Eichenberg over C Creed Humphrey or LB Nick Bolton in 2021 Round 2 • CB Cam Smith over OLB Tuli Tuipulotu or G O'Cyrus Torrence or TE Tyler Kraft in 2023 Round 2 • OLB Chop Robinson over CB Quinyon Mitchell in 2024 Round 1
-- The Dolphins also made a lot of high-profile trades under Grier when they decided to go all in to try to make a deep run into the playoffs and came up short. In that department, the Dolphins got mostly decent value in most of those trades and it's difficult to complain about Grier's work if the mandate was to go for it.
In retrospect, giving up a first-round pick for Bradley Chubb was a questionable (or bad) move because the edge defender was an impact player for only one season, and that 2023 season ended prematurely because of his Week 17 knee injury.
The Tyreek Hill trade can be debated for a while, but it's impossible to call it an out-and-out miss for Miami.
Likewise, it's difficult to criticize the terms of the Jalen Ramsey trade after getting him for a third-round pick and a backup tight end, but the question is whether Grier should have known his personality could be an issue at some point.
The reality is that Grier usually got good value in the trades he orchestrated, with the caveat that it helps when the team is willing to make a financial commitment to a player whose team doesn't want to do that.
-- His best trade in terms of value probably was the huge Laremy Tunsil deal with the Houston Texans in the rebuild of 2019 that netted the Dolphins all sorts of high draft picks.
-- The Dolphins also got great value in a draft trade involving picks in 2021 draft when they got two future first-round picks to move down from 3 to 12, but from this vantage point that win was somewhat negated when they turned around and traded one of those future No. 1s to move back up to 6. And then it also says here the Dolphins made a mistake by taking Jaylen Waddle, even though he's a very good wide receiver, instead of Penei Sewell, who has become an elite tackle on his way to the Hall of Fame.
-- Grier did hit on some draft picks during his time, never more than his very first draft when the Dolphins landed Tunsil in the first round and Xavien Howard in the second. Christian Wilkins was a good first-round pick in 2019, and other hits have included Robert Hunt in Round 2 in 2020, De'Von Achane in Round 3 in 2023, Malik Washington in Round 6 in 2024 and Patrick Paul in Round 2 in 2024 as well.
In the end, though, the misses clearly stood out more than the hits and one year later it's difficult to argue against the decision the Dolphins made because it does appear the organization is on the right path, even though it might take a little bit of time to get there.
While he always took more blame that he probably deserved, it's also very difficult to give Grier a high grade as Dolphins GM.
Let's just say his tenure was uninspiring, though not nearly as bad as a lot of Dolphins fans want to portray it.
Sullivan, meanwhile, can do no wrong in the eyes of a lot of fans right now because of the massive contributions of the rookie class, though the caveat must be included is the fact the roster being stripped provided a lot of immediate opportunities for those young players.
That said, it's really difficult to find fault with many, if any, of the moves he has made so far.
One that stands out was the decision to bypass the popular choice of Rueben Bain Jr. with the Dolphins' first of their two first-round picks. While we're not even at the halfway point of their rookie season, Kadyn Proctor right now has the look of a future star on the offensive line — wherever he winds up lining up — while Bain has done nothing to dispell the concern some draft analysts and media members brought up about his shorter arms being a major detriment as an NFL pass rusher.
The Dolphins regulardly have had six or seven rookies in their starting lineup this season, a testament both to the rebuild and to Sullivan's work.
The real test will come in future years when we see how many of those players remain starters.
Again, though, Sullivan is off to a great start. And for some Dolphins fans, the best part is he's not Chris Grier.

title: Vikings' Biggest Defensive Concern Can Be Solved by a Trade Call With Eagles
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings may have a lot of bodies available on the defensive line, but many of them are struggling to be effective or are young players who need time to develop before they can become major contributors.
Minnesota should be in the market to trade for players to help stay on top of the NFC North and prepare for a hopeful playoff berth. One player who may be available in trade talks is Philadelphia Eagles defensive lineman Moro Ojomo.
Philadelphia selected Ojomo in the seventh round of the 2023 NFL Draft, and he has played 335 defensive snaps for the Eagles this season. Through eight games, he has 21 tackles, four quarterback hits and three tackles for a loss.
The Vikings' defensive line has some solid play this season. Jalen Redmond is ranked tenth among all defensive linemen with a 78 overall Pro Football Focus grade and should be a priority for Minnesota to re-sign. However, other big men in the trenches haven't fared as well as Redmond.
Here are other Vikings' defensive linemen's PFF grades and rankings through eight weeks:
Ojomo has a 57.6 PFF grade, which would give him the third-highest grade on Minnesota's roster. This season, he has generated 18 quarterback pressures and 14 hurries while earning a 57.1 run defense grade.
Standing 6-foot-3 and weighing 292 pounds, Ojomo is a versatile defender in the trenches who could help give the Vikings more time to develop Banks and Orange slowly, and not rush their development, while still being competitive.
Minnesota has struggled to slow down the run lately and has given up long rushing touchdowns in each of its last two games. According to a clip from The Aftermath shared on X by ESPN senior reporter Jeremy Fowler, Ojomo is a player that Minnesota could show interest in acquiring .
Right now, Vikings fans are waiting for Minnesota to make a move. Trading for a quality player right now would prove that the franchise believes that a deep playoff run is possible. Hopefully, the Purple and Gold can get a deal done before the Nov. 10 trade deadline to make the team as competitive as possible for the remainder of the season.

title: Vikings Make Major Blunder With New FA Signing as Trade Deadline Approaches
full_text:
Vikings fans closely monitoring social media for possible trade deadline news may have gotten a bit of a jump scare Wednesday.
NFL Insider Jordan Schultz reported that the Vikings signed offensive lineman Corey Robinson II after he worked out with them, a report later confirmed by the team . The move came one day after the team released backup guard Trevor Keegan.
The #Vikings are signing OL Corey Robinson II after having him in for a workout. Robinson is an undrafted free agent out of Arkansas who was with the Bengals after the draft. https://t.co/4rXR0b61yP pic.twitter.com/5yGs6MNGyQ
Naturally, the move sparked questions and reopened conversations about the need for the team to make serious moves as the trade deadline approaches. Does the move actually make the 2026 Vikings any better?
We’ll have to see, but the timing was certainly odd for several reasons.
Robinson is, for the most part, a complete unknown in the NFL.
The former Arkansas Razorback signed with the Cincinnati Bengals as an undrafted free agent this past April, after starting 12 games at left tackle in 2025. It remains to be seen if the Vikings plan to use him at tackle or on their interior, but is betting on him really the right move after Trevor Keegan’s release on Tuesday left the Vikings without a true backup guard?
It was theorized that Keegan might re-sign with the practice squad, but ESPN ’s Mike Garafolo reported Wednesday afternoon that the Buccaneers claimed him off waivers.
The Vikings may make additional corresponding moves, but this one seems odd in a vacuum.
The #Buccaneers claimed G Trevor Keegan off waivers from the #Vikings .
Left guard Joe Huber is already starting in relief of an injured Donovan Jackson, and Will Fries has been shaky at right guard to start 2026. If either is injured, the Vikings may need to get creative given their lack of depth. An undrafted rookie tackle with no NFL experience does not exactly seem like the ideal backup plan. In the meantime, it’s clear Vikings fans were hoping for much bigger news.
The Vikings are 6-1 with an all-world defense and currently hold the NFC’s second seed. Seems like a perfect time to make a massive move, and in previous years, they probably would. But the long-term cap and roster situation makes things incredibly complicated . Still, most fans naturally want to see the team go all in, especially since so many key veterans may not be around after this season.
For those constantly checking their phones for news, signing a backup offensive lineman likely wasn’t what they hoped to see.
With the Nov. 10 deadline quickly approaching, it seems we’ll all have to wait on the edge of our seats a little longer as we wait for the “big” news to drop… if it ever does.

title: Vikings are Making an Ivan Pace Jr. Mistake as Trade Deadline Looms
full_text:
The Vikings have played seven games this season, and it has become abundantly clear that 25-year-old linebacker Ivan Pace Jr. hasn't been and won't be a major contributor in defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit.
Through those seven games, Pace played a total of 59 defensive snaps, an average of 8.4 defensive snaps per game. Even though he is a regular contributor on special teams and played 152 snaps there (83.5%), it is disappointing not to see him more involved on defense.
For comparison, this is what Pace's defensive snap count looked like in his first three seasons with the Vikings:
Despite the shrinking role, it'd be wise for the Vikings to give Pace some more snaps against the Bills in Week 9. The reason isn't to give Blake Cashman or Eric Wilson time on the sidelines, but to increase his visibility if Minnesota looks to put him on the trade block this year.
With Cashman and Wilson cemented into the Vikings' starting interior linebacker positions and rookie Jake Golday developing to be a future contributor at the position, Pace is struggling to get defensive snaps this year.
Pace could be a trade asset for Minnesota, but the Purple and Gold aren't going to raise his value by sitting him on the sideline. He used to be a starter for the Vikings (27 times in 52 appearances, to be exact. As an undrafted free agent in 2023, he recorded 102 tackles and 2.5 sacks,
Since that rookie year, his playing time and his stats have decreased with each passing season. Last year, he started only six games, but still had 62 tackles, two tackles for a loss, and one sack. His recent play has proven that he can be productive in a limited role.
However, now is not the time to let Pace spend so much time on the bench. Getting him some defensive action over the next few games could go a long way toward increasing his trade value, potentially allowing Minnesota to get an asset for him instead of allowing him to leave as a free agent after this season.
Pace is currently on a one-year, $3.52 million contract with the Vikings, but is unlikely to re-sign the former Miami (OH) and Cincinnati defender as long as the team has Cahman, Wilson and Golday on the roster. Another team could view his expiring deal as a chance to take a swing on a low-risk yet experienced rental.
There are defensive-needy teams out there that could use a young linebacker like Pace to hold down the middle of their defense. His age, history of production, and potential say a lot about what he has to offer, but the NFL is a league that is based on what a player has done recently.
Sadly, he hasn't been asked to do much in the Vikings' defense lately, giving the Purple and Gold all the reason to display him to potential suitors this weekend.
