title: 4 Boxes Titans Must Check Over Bye Week: Holding Off on 1 Trade, Offensive Changes, and More
full_text:
The Titans enter the bye week at a perfect time. The players are undoubtedly ready for a break after going non-stop since the end of July. It also gives the Titans time to really evaluate what’s working and what isn’t so they can try to make the necessary changes after the break.
And with the trade deadline next Tuesday, this time off also gives them the time to truly evaluate some of the offers that are undoubtedly coming in.
This article is going to discuss four things the Titans need to prioritize coming out of the bye, including which player to trade, who to hold onto, and what changes to make. With that said, let’s not waste anymore time and dive right into it.
Trade interest in the Titans’ running back appears to be at an all-time high after Pollard totaled 292 yards from scrimmage (246 rushing, 46 receiving) and five touchdowns over his last two games.
Because of this, the Titans will have to weigh the pros and cons of keeping Pollard around for at least the rest of the season. The unfortunate truth is that the Memphis product is on an expiring contract and will likely head elsewhere this offseason.
So, the Titans would obviously benefit from getting something in return while they still can. On the flip side of things, they also have to consider how a trade like that would impact their young quarterback.
Titans QB Cam Ward is coming off the best game of his career , topping 300 yards for the first time, while nearly out-dueling the Bengals’ high-powered offense. Dan Orlovsky dubbed his tape as the best of the week.
Had the best Sunday QB tape in the NFL @Titans #nfllive pic.twitter.com/GOiRQurhyd
But part of that success came because they had a balanced attack that kept Cincinnati’s defense guessing. Trading Pollard away leaves this offense at risk of being extremely one-dimensional, especially with RB Tyjae Spears’ inability to stay on the field.
Therefore, I don’t believe they should just give Pollard away for the sake of getting something in return. Ward’s development means way more to this franchise than getting another mid-round pick. Unless someone offers a late day two pick, which I personally think is unlikely, I believe it would be wise to just stay put and help your young quarterback as much as you can.
One thing that stood out about the Titans’ approach last Sunday was how quickly they operated offensively throughout the contest.
According to Next Gen Stats , approximately 41.4 percent of their snaps (29) came out of no huddle — most of any team in any game this season, and the results were undeniable. The Titans averaged 8.5 yards per play when using no huddle, which is 3.2 yards more than the league average of 5.3.
They also eclipsed 400 yards of offense for the first time this season, totaling 440 yards against the Bengals, which was their highest yardage output of the season and nearly 200 yards more than their average of 248.5 YPG heading into Week 8.
It’s clear this is a formula that works for Ward, so we should be seeing more of it after the bye if the Titans are to compete on a higher level and give their QB a chance to fully break out.
This is arguably the biggest change that needs to happen. To say the acquisition of WR Wan’Dale Robinson hasn’t worked out as planned would be a massive understatement.
Robinson signed a lucrative $70 million deal last offseason to help solidify the Titans’ slot position for the foreseeable future. Unfortunately, that investment has only led to 262 receiving yards, three touchdowns, and a handful of brutal drops through eight games. The former Kentucky Wildcat currently has a drop rate of six percent, which is the highest of his career and nearly double his career average (3.9).
And then there’s WR Calvin Ridley. Rumors are circulating that there is somewhat of a trade market for Ridley, and if that’s the case, they absolutely should take whatever they can get and move on. Ridley has only produced six catches for 91 yards this season, and even when he is targeted, it’s a toss-up whether or not he’ll actually reel it in.
Meanwhile, with Tate out last Sunday, second-year WRs Ayomanor and Dike combined for eight catches, 107 yards, and one touchdown; a clear upgrade over anything Robinson and Ridley have done all year. As for Tate, he enters the bye week leading all rookie receivers (and the team for that matter) with 413 receiving yards despite missing last week’s game with a shoulder injury.
It’s plain that Tennessee misjudged the potential of their young trio in comparison to the people they brought in and retained.
A divorce with at least Ridley, if not also Robinson, feels inevitable at the end of the season. That leaves no reason not to commit to the youth movement after the bye break. It would be wise to start giving the guys who will actually be here beyond this season all of the reps they can get to help set them up for success going into 2027.
Will Dike and Ayomanor ever develop into bona fide starting-caliber receivers? Only time will tell. But right now, they’re clearly the two most consistent targets outside of Tate, so don’t be surprised to see plenty more of them going forward, and less of the overpriced veterans.
The Titans’ second-year TE has really made his presence felt over the last two weeks, reeling in eight catches for 100 yards, including a team-high 76 yards last Sunday.
Those numbers may seem modest, but compared to his production earlier this season, it’s a massive improvement. Helm totaled just 60 receiving yards over the team’s first five games, including a two-game stretch where he combined for just five yards.
That’s simply unacceptable for someone as reliable as Helm is in the passing game. He gives Ward a big body to target in the middle of the field, especially on third downs. Ward has developed a real trust in him in those scenarios, largely due to Helm’s large catch radius and soft hands.
What's more, now that Tate is returning to the lineup, things could really start to open up for Helm as long as OC Brian Daboll continues to make him a priority in the offense. If that’s the case, we should be seeing his numbers look closer to what they did over the last two weeks as opposed to what they were at the start of the season.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: Titans Refusing to Trade Their Best Defender Twice in 1 Month Should Give Fans a Sigh of Relief
full_text:
Trade rumors are at an all-time high now. Less than one week away from the NFL's trade deadline set for Nov. 10, the Tennessee Titans are one of the teams being tabbed with the potential to be active ahead of the deadline.
It was reported on Wednesday morning that Tennessee isn't looking to trade S Amani Hooker despite interest from teams around the league, per ESPN's Jeremy Fowler.
The Titans are less than a week removed from dealing their franchise best player, DT Jeffery Simmons, and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Chicago Bears for two future first-round picks and a 2027 fourth-round pick. Simmons has been one of the hottest names mentioned at the deadline for several years, and the Titans finally made it a done deal.
After the Simmons trade, the Titans named Hooker a defensive captain for the remainder of the season, according to Jim Wyatt .
Last week against the Cincinnati Bengals, Hooker had the best game of his career with a Simmons-less defense. The eight-year safety secured three interceptions on Bengals' QB Joe Burrow, a career-high. He became the first Titan since S Kevin Byard on Oct. 22, 2017, to record three interceptions in a single game.
Interestingly enough, Byard, a former teammate of Hooker's, was the most recent safety the franchise has traded. Back at the 2023 NFL trade deadline, the Eagles swapped S Terrell Edmunds and two draft picks for the then two-time First Team All-Pro, Byard.
However, it appears the Titans will hold onto their 28-year-old safety despite being named one of the expected mid-season targets by contenders looking to strike a deal. Hooker has had a career year this season, already tying his season-high of five interceptions, which he last accomplished in 2024. He leads all NFL defenders with five interceptions, two more than the second-place holders.
Both drafted in 2019, losing Hooker and Simmons in the same season would certainly change the outlook of the Titans' defense, especially for a defensive-minded head coach in Robert Saleh. Hooker leads the Titans with six passes deflected and has the second most tackles on the team.
In addition to being one of the most experienced players on the defense, Hooker's experience is invaluable for younger players.
If the Titans are to strike anymore deals at the deadline, it may come from the offensive side of the ball. Only time will tell, but it looks like Hooker will stay in Nashville - and that's a good thing.
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: A Deep Dive Into Cam Ward's Career Game vs. Bengals Reveals 3 Key Signs of Life Moving Forward
full_text:
Last week against the Bengals in Cincinnati, QB Cam Ward willed himself to the best performance of his professional career.
Ward led the Titans to score 36 points, throwing for two touchdowns, which is the highest scoring game for the franchise in five years. It marked a career-high 304 yards passing for Ward while snapping a five-game interception streak.
It made Ward the first Tennessee quarterback to throw for more than 300 yards, two touchdowns and zero interceptions since Ryan Fitzpatrick on Nov. 24, 2013 .
Ward was able to accomplish these feats without his best target WR Carnell Tate, who was sidelined with a shoulder injury. Heading into the matchup, Tate led the Titans and his 2026 draft class in receiving yards and receptions.
There has been immense pressure placed on Ward to live up to his first overall expectations after a rocky rookie season. While the second-year pro hasn't made the leap many fans or pundits expected, he reminded everyone why he's a starting quarterback in the NFL by going toe-to-toe with Cincinnati's QB Joe Burrow on Sunday.
Here's a breakdown of what made Ward successful against the Bengals in a beat-by-beat recap of the game, even with the odds stacked against him.
As was noted, Ward threw no interceptions against Cincinnati, and it was the most accurate he's been all season.
The 6'2" QB completed 26 of 40 attempts for a 65% completion percentage, tying his season-high that was set Week 2 against the New York Jets. However, in New York, he only threw 20 passes.
Ward began the first quarter, completing 10 of his first 13 passes, including five passes for more than 10 yards. He only had one missed throw in that stretch. One of the incompletions came from a dropped pass that hit the hands of a wide-open WR Calvin Ridley, and another was a throwaway.
Unfortunately, the Titans have the second most drops by any team this season, with 18, according to Pro Football Reference . Tennessee took a convincing 13-0 lead in the first quarter.
In the second, Ward completed four straight passes, including three passes for at least 13 yards to move Tennessee into the Bengals' territory. On the fourth completion, WR Wan'Dale Roninson bobbled a pass on a bubble screen that was ruled a fumble, ending the Titans' promising drive with a turnover.
Following a fumble on the opening drive of the second half by Ward, he drove Tennessee down, completing all four of his passes, including an in-stride pass to WR Chimere Dike for 28 yards to put the Titans in the red zone.
Tennessee would score on that drive with a goal-line rushing touchdown by RB Tony Pollard, capped off by a Ward 2-point conversion to tie the game 21-21 in the third. In the beginning of the fourth, the Titans topped off on a four-play drive where Ward split two Cincinnati defenders to hit Dike for an 11-yard passing touchdown. The score swung the lead back in Tennessee's favor 28-23.
On the next drive, Tennesse drove 68 yards down the field with a mix of runs and passes. Finished off with a perfectly placed dart on the back shoulder of Robinson, away from the guarding Bengals' defender, for a 15-yard touchdown.
While backpedaling away from Bengals rushers, Ward found TE Gunnar Helm in the end zone to complete another 2-point conversion. It gave the Titans a 36-29 lead with less than four minutes left in the game.
The Bengals would go on to put up 14 unanswered points and escape with a 36-29 win. Across Ward's 40 attempts, none of his passes were closely intercepted by a Bengals defender.
Per PFF , the Tennessee quarterback had an adjusted completion of 80% that removes dropped passes, throwaways and batted passes. By PFF standards, Ward only missed on eight of his 40 attempts. It's important to note Ward also threw for five passes for more than 20 yards, which is a career-high total.
Against Cincinnati, Ward recorded a career-high 41 rushing yards. He and Ravens' QB Lamar Jackson are the only quarterbacks to throw for at least 300 yards and rush for 40 yards this season.
Despite being pressured on more than 30% of his dropbacks, the former Miami Hurricane only took two sacks. It's important to note those two sacks were pivotal. One resulted in a fumble, and the other pushed Tennessee out of field goal range at the end of regulation.
Nonetheless, Ward was far more mobile against the Bengals than he had been up to that point.
In the first quarter, he tucked the ball to convert a fourth-and-one on the Tennessee side of the field. Ward faked a sweeping handoff to Pollard and leaped over two Bengals defenders to convert on third down early in the second quarter.
On another third-and-short, Ward kept the ball on an option play with Pollard, resulting in a 14-yard gain in the third quarter. Later in the quarter, Ward spun past Bengals defenders to score a 2-point conversion. In the fourth quarter, Ward evaded the Cincinnati pass rushers to complete his second 2-point conversion of the game with a pass to Helm to give the Titans the lead late.
Ward drove Titans down the field consistently, producing a season-high of 440 yards on offense. The Ward-led offense stayed on the field for a season-high time of 32 minutes and 11 seconds. Two weeks ago, the Titans were dead last in average time of possession per game because of their inability to move the ball down the field consistently.
Ward produced four of the Titans' five third-down conversions. Three of the conversions were from passes and one from a run. Furthermore, Ward converted a fourth down from a 14-yard rush and scored on a 2-point conversion twice, one on the ground and the other in the air.
Tennessee's offense was more explosive against the Bengals than it's been all season because Ward was beating the defense with a dual-threat approach. Ward showed that he can beat defenses with the pass and the run, which proved to keep the Titans on the field and in the game against a heavily favored Bengals team.
These are the signs of life Tennesse needed to see from Ward. Week 8 was the most important yet in his young NFL career.
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: Why Titans' Reported Asking Price for WR Calvin Ridley Toes the Line Between Smart and Stubborn
full_text:
This morning, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler released his latest batch of NFL trade buzz as we rapidly approach the November 10 deadline. As is the natural state of a team in the middle of a multi-year rebuild, the Tennessee Titans received their own bulky treatment from the insider.
At the center of the noise is, unsurprisingly, WR Calvin Ridley. "Ridley is considered a backup plan for a few teams in the receiver market..." wrote Fowler. "The sense I get from talking to teams is the Titans would need a quality Day 3 pick to part with Ridley, whose $13 million in 2026 cash could be a hurdle based on his low production."
While Tennessee isn't eager to make a trade, Ridley having essentially fallen out of contention in the Titans' offense demands his availability, at the very least. Tennessee wasn't looking to trade Jeffery Simmons either, but here we are.
If we're talking about a fifth-round pick for Ridley, what's the read on that asking price? Well, whether or not that's a fair tag will depend entirely on the buyer. If push comes to shove at the deadline, I believe the Titans should move Ridley no matter what... but you can't blame them for holding out.
In general, it's be difficult to argue that Ridley is playing up to the worth of a fifth-rounder this season. He's only managed to pull in six receptions in eight games, and hasn't yet broken 100 yards. The 31-year old has only missed one contest. This is a matter of poor production.
However, Ridley signed with Tennessee just two years ago for $92 million. That contract has since been restructured, but he's only one year removed from a 1,000-yard, four-score showing. It's not hard to see why teams in need of a pass-catcher has logged him as an option.
Sometimes, it's simply a matter of a player expiring in the specific scenario they're in. In reality, Ridley's time in Nashville was toast the moment the Titans drafted Carnell Tate. Between the rookie WR, $70 million signee Wan'Dale Robinson, and second-year playmakers Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike, it's not in the cards for Ridley with Tennessee anymore.
He's not even playing for the same regime that signed him.
That's why, from a personnel perspective, the Titans shouldn't be picky about their return here. Getting anything at all for Ridley at this point would benefit the rebuild and shed an asset that doesn't fit the picture any longer.
If there are truly multiple interested suitors that Tennessee wants to take down to the wire, go for it by all means. But by the deadline, it'd be unnecessarily stubborn of general manager Mike Borgnozi to hold on to the WR. The question should be "move now or move soon?" instead of "should we move at all?"
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Making the Case for Titans Taking a First-Round RB in 2027: The Perfect Tony Pollard Succession Plan
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans have a slow-rising problem that must be addressed in the backfield. For the time being, it's looking less and less likely that veteran RB Tony Pollard will be traded. He seemed like a surefire candidate entering the year, but Pollard's dominant play as of late demands otherwise.
That, and his usual second-hand-man, in Tyjae Spears, has been a non-factor this season. In six games this year, Spears has just 18 carries for 66 yards. He's added 15 receptions for 75 yards, two fumbles, and no scores.
Spears has consistently missed practices, most recently with a knee issue, and has fallen almost entirely out of the rotation even when he's active. Between Spears and rookie back Nick Singleton, the backfield looked like the least of Tennessee's futuristic worries prior to this season.
Now, as far as 2027 is concerned, it may be one of their biggest. Even if Tennessee doesn't trade Pollard by the deadline this year, the 29-year old is in the final year of his contract. Odds are slim that  Tennessee would sign him to a multi-year deal entering his 30s.
So, what is the best plan of action here? I'd argue that it isn't to wait on Spears, but to take the punch in the gut and draft another back next year.
No, this wouldn't mean Tennessee admits defeat with the Singleton pick. After all, the Penn State alumnus was a fifth-round pick and should've been seen as a project to begin with.
But take one look at the free agent slate for next season and tell me Tennessee has a better option. You're looking at a series of veteran backs beyond their primes; Alvin Kamara (31), Aaron Jones (31), and, of course, Pollard highlight the market. From there, it's mostly multi-year backups more likely to stay put than anything else.
Unless Spears takes a sudden fourth-year leap in the middle of his worst season yet as a Titan, it's time to look forward and take another swing. If Tennessee manages to draft a Jeffery Simmons replacement for the defense with their higher first-round pick, I've got an idea for the later selection.
Enter: Florida RB Jadan Baugh.
I spent all offseason harping on Tennessee to take Jeremiyah Love out of Notre Dame. Everyone is thrilled with Carnell Tate at the WR spot, including me, but the sensibility of going high on a long-term back remains clear.
NFLDraftBuzz.com predicts Baugh to land as a late first-round pick, slotting in as the favored RB1 in a draft class loaded with playmaking talent. Through eight games with the Gators this season, the junior has gone for 801 yards on 152 carries, scoring 13 touchdowns in the process.
Baugh hasn't fumbled the ball once this season. In fact, in three years with Florida, Baugh has only fumbled one time. The big-body back moves extremely well and maintains balance through contact; he's drawing early comparisons to Le'Veon Bell for a reason.
If the argument for keeping Pollard around past the deadline this season is that he's essential to Cam Ward's development, that same ideal should extend to investing in a long-term back to grow alongside Ward. To that end, Baugh is a dream pickup.
Of course, this all depends on whether or not he'd be available when the Titans' late-first (via the Chicago Bears) came to pass. But it seems like this will be a possibility come draft night, at least. If that's the case, I'd love to see Tennessee fully commit to a young backfield and take this stud.
If you're scratching your head wondering what a move like this would mean for Singleton... don't!
I'm as interested in the potential of Singleton as anyone else, but again, a fifth-round pick isn't drafted to be a plug-n-play starter in case something goes wrong. This is firmly a "wait and see" scenario for Tennessee, evidenced by veteran back Michael Carter getting midseason looks over the rookie.
If anything, some young competition would be good for the former Nittany Lion. Draft Baugh, give Singleton the offseason to develop and sharpen iron, keep one of Spears and Carter around as the resident veteran, and roll into the 2027 campaign with a refreshed ground game.
It's a future-facing approach that I think best suits the Titans' rebuild around Ward under center. Given a little luck on draft night, it's something that could realistically come to pass.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans NFL Trade Deadline Big Board: 7 Realistic Pieces Tennessee Could Still Trade
full_text:
The NFL's trade deadline is only six days away now, and the Tennessee Titans have been tabbed as potential sellers time and time again. Moving on from DT Jeffery Simmons certainly filled that cup to some extent, but there are still pieces on the board that look like potential trades.
As of yesterday, Tennessee doesn't look eager to make any moves. But there are guys that arguably should be sent out anyway, and others the team could trade, but would be better off keeping.
To compile everything into one spot, we've put together a Titans trade big board as your one-stop-shop for the latest on deadline possibilities. So far as anyone can tell, here are the players we could see Tennessee shop by November 10.
Ridley appears like the most likely trade candidate on this roster, and there's a real discussion to be had about the necessity of moving on from the veteran WR.
With just six catches for 91 yards on the season, Ridley's role in Tennessee's offense has clearly expired. Although, to a contending team with a need at the position, the 31-year old's value is more apparent.
A team like the Pittsburgh Steelers or the Kansas City Chies come to mind. This is not a ranked list, but Ridley still had to be mentioned at the top of it. It seems fair to say that no player fits the bill of a possible trade more than Ridley. The Titans have six days to get something, anything, done.
Coming off his three-interception performance against the Cincinnati Bengals (Hooker leads the NFL with five total), the Titans' veteran S has spiked his value. He looked like the best player in Robert Saleh's defense in Week 8.
Hooker, 29, has ground himself as a consistently reliable presence in the secondary. He appeals to contending teams for the same reasons that Ridley does, only Hooker is inarguably better at his position.
Tennessee should likely think twice about trading Hooker, especially after moving off one of their defensive anchors already. Under contract through 2028, the possibility of moving Hooker could be kicked down the road until the Titans' rebuild is a little more fleshed out.
All the same, for the right offer, it would make sense if Tennessee decided to double down on their draft capital in the coming two seasons.
Pollard appears to be the least likely to be traded of the bunch at this point. Coming into the season, it appeared that Tyjae Spears was set to succeed Pollard due to the latter being in the final year of his contract.
But Pollard has removed any doubt from his role as RB1 in Nashville. He's taken what began as a backfield split and turned it into a one-man-show. Pollard has five rushing scores and nearly 250 yards combined over the past two games.
That means his value is at an all-time high, but the veteran RB now slots in as a critical cog in Cam Ward's offensive machine. Tennessee would certainly have buyers for Pollard, especially if and when someone lands star RB Jonathan Taylor.
However, if Pollard is tied to Ward finally breaking out - as he did last week - risking throwing the QB off his course doesn't seem worth it. This one looks less likely by the day.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported last week that teams " in the market for an edge rusher believe Johnson could be available at the right price." Johnson was brought to Nashville in a trade this past offseason, and is playing in the final year of his rookie deal that originated with the New York Jets.
Johnson has three sacks this season and has been a fair contributor on Tennessee's defensive line. When Simmons was traded, Saleh tabbed Johnson as a potential emerging leader in his wake.
With ties to Saleh due to their shared time together in New York and Tennessee having just shed their best d-lineman, Johnson looks like a less serious candidate now than he did before the Simmons ordeal.
But the right price is the right price, and on defense, the Titans could be more likely to hit the reset button while Ward figures things out on the other side of the ball. That point is evidenced by the rest of this list.
Taylor pretty well removed himself from most trade discussions this past week. The offseason pickup, who was benched as recently as Week 6, posted a comeback performance fueled by his move from the outside to nickel.
On top of that, CB Marcus Harris injured his ankle and left the game; if Harris misses time, Taylor will be Tennessee's go-to option at nickel. He went from an obvious trade possibility to someone who looks almost immovable for the time being.
Taylor deserved a mention here due to how up and down his season has been, but he's closer to Pollard than Ridley as far as likelihood goes.
Martin is a similar candidate to the aforementioned Hooker. Where Hooker had three picks, Martin had three sacks against Cincinnati. The latter is a 30-year old veteran with an impressive journeyman resume that landed in Tennessee on a two-year deal.
He's sitting at 6.5 sacks on the season right now, which is already a career-high. The Titans are just halfway through their 2026 campaign.
As our own Dharya Sharma noted, Martin has risen into full blue-chip status as a trade potential. But like Johnson, he's now a primary playmaker with Simmons in the rearview. One or the other could be traded, but with DL John Franklin-Myers playing through a back injury, holding on to both seems like the safe play.
Finally, we come to LB Cody Barton. A 29-year old veteran who has steadily seen his snaps taper off this year, Barton now appears at risk of losing his spot on the inside to Cedric Gray, who is 24.
Once rookie Anthony Hill Jr. came on the scene and made it clear that he was the best LB on this Titans team, less surefire snaps were being divvied heavily in Barton's favor after Cedric Gray missed Week 1 with a concussion.
Barton remained in control up until a few weeks ago, when Gray's looks began to chip away at Barton's. Gray was one of the NFL's leading tacklers last season, and it seemed like only a matter of time before he re-assumed a similar role in Saleh's defense.
If Tennessee trusts Gray to succeed Barton, moving the latter would seem like the natural next step.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Deadline Debate: Do Titans Trade Tony Pollard at Peak Value, or Keep Him for Cam Ward's Sake?
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans' offense had its best game of the 2026 NFL season on Sunday, scoring 36 points in a losing effort to the Cincinnati Bengals.
Despite suffering their seventh loss of the year, the Titans were firing on all cylinders offensively in Week 8, especially quarterback Cam Ward and running back Tony Pollard. Ward threw for 304 yards and two touchdowns on 65% completion , while Pollard rushed for 117 yards and two scores on 5.6 yards per carry.
With Tennessee sitting at 1-7 and having already traded All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, many have assumed the Titans are willing to deal some of their veteran talent. Pollard has been a name often mentioned in potential trade discussions, but the Titans may be better off keeping him.
Pollard has been one of the most consistent running backs in the NFL over the last few years, and has been elite in recent weeks. The 29-year-old has tallied 246 rushing yards and five touchdowns in the past two games and is top-ten in rushing yards (595) and touchdowns (6) this year.
As a result, Pollard's trade value is higher than it has ever been . A contending team that is looking to elevate its rushing attack may have interest in a savvy veteran back in Pollard, who is in the final year of his deal with Nashville. From the outside looking in, the chips are falling for a sensible trade.
With the Titans still rebuilding, it would make sense to move Pollard and acquire picks for the future. However, Tennessee should also heavily consider retaining the former Pro Bowler. Pollard is critical to Ward's development, as supplying a young quarterback with a stable run game is always a fantastic plan. Pollard makes Ward's life easier and sets up play-action passes, which Ward has had success with.
Ward looked comfortable this past week because, in part, he was freed up by Pollard's ground game. Especially with complimentary options like Tyjae Spears and Nick Singleton fading into the background, Pollard has worked himself into an important and singular role this season.
Overall, trading Pollard before the November 10 deadline wouldn't be a surprising move from general manager Mike Borgonzi, but keeping him to support Ward and help the offense afloat for the rest of the season looks like the more viable avenue right now for Tennessee.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Titans Reportedly Unlikely to Make More Trades — But Calvin Ridley Should be Moved at Any Cost
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans cutting a deal with the Chicago Bears to move franchise-defining DT Jeffery Simmons made the trade deadline look far less dire. Nobody expected the Titans to end up with two first-round picks with any of their other assets, after all.
But sometimes, making trades isn't all about the capital you get in return. Guys can be moved because their value has peaked, because they don't fit the scheme any longer, or both. Veteran receiver Calvin Ridley falls into the third category.
Today, Terry McCormick reported that "the Titans are not likely to make more trades, unless an offer over fair market value comes their way." However, Ridley should be moved no matter the return, save for something truly outlandish.
Ridley was brought to Nashville back in 2024 on an unimaginable four-year, $92 million deal. He's struggled to stay on the field since his first season, and even when Ridley does participate, his production is buried beneath talent younger than him.
The former Alabama sensation has shown flashes since his move to Nashville; after all, he surpassed 1,000 yards receiving in his first campaign. But it's undeniable that Ridley is a remnant of the Brian Callahan era. That's a time this franchise is still scratching and clawing to move past.
Ridley came into this season competing directly with rookie sensation Carnell Tate, big-name signee Wan'Dale Robinson, and second-year risers Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike. For him to start in Week 1, even after restructuring his contract in the offseason, was surprising.
The 31-year old receiver has since made it clear that he's not at home in this rotation. Ridley dropped his fourth ball of the season in Week 8 against the Cincinnati Bengals. He'd finish the contest with one reception on just three targets, and that was without Tate playing at all.
Ridley has just six receptions on the year for 91 yards. In Week 8, the aforementioned Dike had five catches for 71 yards. His steady decline in snaps has him at 218 on the year, per FantasyPros. For reference, Wan'Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate sit at 334 and 329, respectively.
As long as Ridley is getting work, he's taking valuable looks away from the likes of Ayomanor and Dike. The Titans, in an effort to fully commit to building a future-forward team around Cam Ward under center, should have Ridley at the tip-top of their trade block.
If that means taking a late-draft pick to move off an asset whose contract will expire next season anyways? So be it. Ridley was once an exciting prospect in Nashville, and he deserves credit for reworking his contract to remain a Titan for a little while longer.
But we're halfway through the 2026 season. With the November 10 deadline looming ahead, this is a need that has made itself painfully clear. Trade Ridley to a willing contender in need of playmaking help (see the Kansas City Chiefs, for example) wipe your hands, and press on.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: 3 Bold Predictions for Titans After Bye Week: Is a Late-Season Winning Streak Realistic?
full_text:
We've officially hit the midway point of the Tennessee Titans' 2026 season as bye week is next on the schedule. The team is 1-7, but last week's defeat on the road against the Cincinnati Bengals yielded more positivity than negativity for the Robert Saleh era.
Moving forward, this team still has a whole lot to prove, and they'll have to prove it without star DT Jeffery Simmons. The outlook is presently bleak in Nashville, but if last week is a real indicator, the future is bright.
Regarding the future, I'm making three bold predictions for the rest of this season to ruminate in your mind as bye week comes to pass. Here are a few notes on what I believe will be an improved part two to Tennessee's campaign.
The Tennessee Titans falling just short to the Cleveland Browns in Week 7 cut short the team's chances of winning their first back-to-back games since 2022. However, I believe that curse will finally be lifted in December.
On the 20th and 27th respectively, the Titans play the Indianapolis Colts (home) and Las Vegas Raiders (away). Tennessee already beat the Colts once, marking their only victory of the season. Indianapolis has since initiated an apparent fire sale on the trade market and fired their general manager. Indy is 2-6 overall right now.
The Raiders, on the other hand, are 4-4. The team is vastly improved under first-year head coach Klint Kubiak, but after starting 0-3, the wheels have begun to fall off for Las Vegas. With ongoing discussions about Kirk Cousins' starting role at QB, they're very much in flux as a franchise.
Tennessee would certainly have to get hot late, especially on the road against the Raiders. But a bold take is a bold take, and having already come so close to breaking this historically bad streak, I believe it's fair to predict that the Titans won't waste such a close shave again. This window looks like their best shot.
With leading WR Carnell Tate out in Week 8 due to a shoulder injury, it was second-year pass-catcher Chimere Dike who stepped into the positional spotlight. Dike looked fantastic vs. Cincy.
The Pro-Bowl returner logged five catches for 71 yards and a second-half touchdown. As a result of his immediate impact in the offense, I'm predicting that Dike ascends all the way up into the WR2 spot for Tennessee.
Behind Tate, it makes sense to prioritize a young playmaker in Tennessee's ongoing rebuild. Dike is a great separator, and a look at his film ( per Drew Beatty ) reveals an ability to maintain speed and pick up consistent YAC. Wan'Dale Robinson's struggles make this end all the more probable.
Especially if the Titans move on from Calvin Ridley, Dike should be the first to get extended looks. His massive uptick in snaps last week was made good by a knockout showing. This should only be the beginning of Dike's rise in Brian Daboll's offense.
Cam Ward had his first 300-yard game in Week 8. For the first time this year, Ward fully looked like the franchise QB Tennessee drafted him to be. In the spirit of optimism, I'm predicting that Ward goes on to surpass 3,000 yards again this year on his way to a redemptive campaign.
Ward still has a lot of work to do to overcome a mostly poor first seven games. What had previously been seen in only flashes came out in full force as Ward threw for two scores and went without an interception. He led the Titans to 36 points, the most the team had scored in nearly six years.
There's something to that. There's something to Ward. If Dike is to elevate and Tennessee is to post a late-season winning streak, Ward will have to make his Week 8 showing less irregular. I'm predicting that he does just that, and that his progress reflects in a second straight 3,000-yard year.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Robert Saleh vs. Brian Callahan: How Saleh's First Titans Season Compares, and How He Can Finish Better
full_text:
Robert Saleh is 1-7 through his first eight games as the Titans' head coach. Brian Callahan went 2-6 through his first eight games with Tennessee. Callahan was fired six games into his second season, when the team was 1-5. Callahan finished 4-19 overall before the Titans let him go.
Their records may be similar, but Saleh's first half-season on the sidelines in Nashville feels much different than Callahan's. Now that we've hit the midway point of the 2026 season, it's time for a side-by-side comparison.
Not only are we conducting a progress report of sorts for Saleh, but we'll also lay out reasons to show that the rest of his tenure has the potential to be much different - to be much better.
One-to-two wins being the groundwork for either coach in this comparison is, of course, a terrible start. Even if there's hope to be had with Saleh, it's completely fair to recognize that this Titans team is one loss away from the worst possible start under him.
Of the Titans' eight contests this season, six have been decided in one-score fashion, including the Titans' Week 6 win over the Indianapolis Colts. Tennessee has scored 20+ points four times, and 30+ once.
Looking back to 2024, the results were less predictable. Through eight contests, only four were decided by one score. Tennessee put up 20+ points twice, and 30+ only once. On the surface, Saleh's Titans are playing closer games, and yet losing slightly more.
Even the Titans' 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans this year pales in comparison to the 52-14 drubbing Callahan's team took on the road vs. the Detroit Lions in 2024. Saleh has openly noted that Tennessee has to capitalize late.
The thing with Callahan's opening run? He had the Titans at 3-8 after a Week 12 victory on the road in Houston. After that improbable win, he'd go on to drop six straight to finish the campaign, and 11 of his next 12.
In fact, the very next game after his last win of 2024 was a 42-19 blowout at the hands of the Washington Commanders. The wheels completely fell off for now-released QB Will Levis, who threw three interceptions in that stretch and, at one point in December, two games without a score.
Mason Rudolph playing fill-in under center did Callahan's problematic play-calling no favors. Titans fans will surely remember the former HC giving up his play-calling duties just weeks before he was relieved in Nashville. That through-line haunted him well into year two.
Of course, Saleh is calling plays on the defensive side of the ball, and that's unlikely to change. Amani Hooker's three interceptions this past week didn't cover up the 43 points Saleh's defense allowed. He has his own issues in the opposite respect.
Saleh's 2026 squad appears both a step behind (being short one win) and a step ahead of Callahan's 2024 bunch. The Titans' present-day games are demonstrably closer on a weekly basis, and Cam Ward's performance from last week revived expectations that he'll be a long-term guy under center.
But Saleh still must succeed where Callahan failed. The successive coach has to find a way to close contests that Tennessee has failed to win up to this point. Three wins is the floor, and it's arguable that topping that dreaded number is the bar.
From here on out, the Titans play the Jacksonville Jaguars twice (once at home, once on the road), the Texans and Colts each one more time, as well as the Cowboys, Commanders, the Lions, the Raiders, and the Steelers.
Unlike Callahan's inaugural team, Saleh's has proven they can hang with just about anyone. Last week's road shootout with the 5-2 Cincinnati Bengals proved that, even when missing primary playmakers, the best version of this roster has elite flashes on either side of the ball.
Much of the makeup of these final nine games will have to do with Ward's progress at QB (a huge help for Saleh if he keeps it up), who else the Titans move before the November 10 deadline (if anyone), and how impactful rookies like Carnell Tate and Anthony Hill Jr. can be down the stretch.
But if these first eight games have taught us anything, it's that Saleh and Tennessee will have plenty of opportunities to win games. At the end of the day, it's success that will put Saleh in a different camp than Callahan.
There are reasons between the lines to expect that Saleh's tenure will end differently than the guy's before him. Because the end of Callahan's first season said so much about where he was heading in Tennessee, these next nine games are absolutely critical for Saleh to get over the hump.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Commanders Daily: A Hall of Fame Rule Change Could Help Doug Williams Reach Canton
full_text:
The Pro Football Hall of Fame announced its five remaining Contributor nominees for the Class of 2027 on Wednesday, including former Washington Redskins quarterback Doug Williams, who currently serves as a senior advisor to Commanders GM Adam Peters. The field started with 42 nominees and has been reduced to this group, which includes Robert Kraft, Ralph Hay, Virginia McCaskey, and John Wooten. The Contributor Subcommittee must still choose a single candidate who advances to the full committee. The Hall announced revised bylaws on September 4 for the Class of 2027 selection process. Under the old Contributor definition, candidates were judged on contributions outside of playing or coaching. The new rules allow their playing and coaching careers to be considered, too. The Hall of Fame's website has this nugget now buried in its bylaws. "Moving forward, a nominee’s full resume, including years as a player and/or coach, may be taken into account." Williams became the first Black quarterback to start and win a Super Bowl, earning MVP honors after throwing for 340 yards and four touchdowns in Washington’s 42–10 victory over Denver on January 31, 1988. He also helped the Tampa Bay Buccaneers make their first three playoff appearances. Over nine NFL seasons, he passed for 16,998 yards , threw 100 touchdown passes along with 93 interceptions, and rushed for 884 yards and 15 touchdowns. Williams also had two stints as head coach at Grambling State, winning four Southwestern Athletic Conference titles. Williams also co-founded the Black College Football Hall of Fame with former NFL quarterback James “Shack” Harris in 2009. His NFL scouting and personnel experience includes Jacksonville, Tampa Bay, and Washington. He returned to the Redskins front office in 2014. His current work alongside Peters includes the draft, free agency, and scouting, but he carries a special relationship with the players, many of whom he mentors. The Contributor Subcommittee will meet virtually on November 17 to select one candidate from the remaining five. That candidate would then advance to the full committee for consideration, where they would need at least 80% approval to be elected. The Class of 2027 will be announced at NFL Honors in February, with enshrinement in Canton in August.

title: Commanders-Rams Injury Report Raises New Concern on Depleted Defensive Line
full_text:
The Washington Commanders released their first Week 9 injury report as the team gears up for its matchup with the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday. Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton practiced fully on Wednesday after being limited throughout last week. A day after the team placed both starting defensive tackles on injured reserve , Shy Tuttle was limited with a shoulder injury. Newton returned to practice last week as the team opened his 21-day practice window while he recovers from a torn pectoral muscle. He was downgraded to OUT before the Eagles game, but Commanders head coach Dan Quinn likes how his return is progressing. "The arrow is going up for sure, and I'm very optimistic for it. But it's important to stack another good week of him in practice and movements." Newton must still be activated from injured reserve before he can play against Los Angeles. Treylon Burks was another name missing from Wednesday's practice, as the receiver continues dealing with the foot injury that left him questionable against Philadelphia . He played anyway and led Washington with 81 receiving yards on three catches, including a 53-yard gain. With Terry McLaurin out for the season, the Commanders need Burks available, but missing Wednesday's practice doesn't necessarily mean he'll be unavailable against Los Angeles. Stefon Diggs also sat out Wednesday, although his absence was listed as rest rather than an injury. John Bates (shoulder) and Sam Cosmi (knee) were limited, while Jayden Daniels (left elbow) and Colson Yankoff (knee) practiced fully. Thursday's injury report should provide a clearer picture of where Burks and Tuttle stand heading into the weekend.

title: Commanders' Unique Usage of Safety Nick Cross Could Have Long-Term Implications
full_text:
Washington Commanders safety Nick Cross has greater alignment diversity than any NFL defender, according to SumerSports data through Week 8. The interesting part is that Cross’ position designation captures only part of what defensive coordinator Daronte Jones asks him to do. So, then the real question becomes: What does Washington gain by moving him around this much? Cross gives Jones a 212-pound safety who can play closer to the run game and be used as a blitzer. He can also move back to a deeper alignment on the next snap. Washington doesn’t have to take him off the field to change his job.
There is no defender in the league who has more alignment diversity than Nick Cross. Daronte Jones has him lined up all over the formation for the Commanders (Data from @SumerSports ) pic.twitter.com/JHgTvkubeU
Washington has more than doubled Cross’ slot-alignment rate from his final season with the Colts, according to Pro Football Focus . His work is now split almost evenly among free safety, the box, and the slot. Last season, nearly half of his snaps came in the box.
Source: PFF. Percentages calculated from 1,111 defensive snaps in 2025 and 233 through Week 8 of 2026. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn discussed Cross’ role Monday after Washington’s 27-10 win over Philadelphia . “And then Nick in this game, I thought, did a really good job, especially when he was playing at Nickel, and he was down by the line of scrimmage. We blitzed him some, John; I thought he had a really good third-down run stop,” Quinn said. Cross earned his two highest overall PFF grades of the season against San Francisco and Philadelphia. The Eagles game was also his strongest in run defense and tackling, backing up what Quinn saw near the line.
Good third-down pressure to get Washington's defense off the field. 7-man pressure front vs. 6 blockers. Philly adjusts for the DBL-A mug and Sonny Styles, while Washington bluffs Sonny and drops Dorance Armstrong. Nice fire zone, creating a free rush for Nick Cross. pic.twitter.com/HlvLQrvai3
Washington showed seven possible rushers against six blockers, but Jones didn’t have to send all seven. Sonny Styles bluffed his rush, Dorance Armstrong dropped into coverage, and Cross came free. As the film above shows, the protection accounted for defenders who weren’t coming, giving Cross a path into the backfield without having to beat a blocker.
Source: PFF. Grades and defensive stops cover all of Cross’ alignments. Quinn emphasized Cross’ communication against Philadelphia. “But most importantly, I really felt his communication in this game, the urgency of what we're looking for from that," Quinn said. "So I thought that was a good step forward as well.” Moving Cross around only helps if the other ten defenders are on the same page. Cross’ work at nickel also gives Jones an alternative to Mike Sainristil , who didn’t play a defensive snap against Philadelphia. Cross still has something to prove in coverage. PFF has charged him with 10 receptions on 11 targets for 69 yards and one touchdown across four appearances, with a 56.2 coverage grade. Those catches averaged 6.9 yards, so opponents haven’t piled up yardage in that sample. The figures include all his coverage work, not just his plays from the slot. If Cross proves he can cover consistently from the slot, Washington could have less need for a dedicated nickel corner. That would give general manager Adam Peters more flexibility to prioritize outside corners or depth elsewhere in the secondary. The Rams game is the next test. Cross’ work over the rest of the season could help determine whether Sainristil has a regular role on defense and which positions Washington needs to address in the offseason. title: Commanders Daily: Washington’s Depleted Front Has More Than Kyren Williams to Handle Against the Rams
full_text:
After missing the 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday night, Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw were both placed on injured reserve Tuesday . Reportedly, it marks the end of the season for Payne, who is dealing with a Jones fracture in his foot; Kinlaw underwent season-ending MCL surgery Tuesday, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Wednesday. It should be noted that without the starting two defensive tackles, the Commanders held the Eagles' depleted team to 91 rushing yards on 29 attempts, including 30 yards on 13 carries from Saquon Barkley, who has been dealing with back and hamstring issues, although he held no game designation against Washington. In place of Payne and Kinlaw, Tim Settle Jr. played 42 snaps (61%), and Shy Tuttle played 32 (46%), along with Byron Cowart, who played 11 (16%) after being elevated from the practice squad to the active roster. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the front seven's work: "I knew the run game on the defensive side was gonna be an important one, so I liked what that looked like of guys setting edges," Quinn said.
The Rams have a couple of backs that need some attention. Sunday, Blake Corum rushed for 73 yards on 11 carries, and Kyren Williams added 56 and a touchdown on 16 carries against the Chargers. Corum added 93 rushing yards the week before against the Raiders and has now scored a touchdown from scrimmage in four consecutive games.
one thing I loved is how mcvay stuck with the hot hand this entire drive, didn’t rotate in kyren at all and just let blake corum take over, whether it’s kyren, or blake… you need to ride the hot hand… pic.twitter.com/vMF4b0Zzwe
Corum can dump yards in spurts. On Sunday, he gained 55 rushing yards on five carries in the opening possession of the second half against the Chargers, including the 23-yard touchdown that gave the Rams a 17-9 lead. The Commanders' rotation will have to stay focused, as the Rams have multiple backs who need the front seven's full attention and aim to wear them down over four quarters. Corum understands what his coach needs out of him: "Our big thing here, Coach McVay always says, is stamina. And so I knew one of them was going to crack," Corum said Sunday . With Payne and Kinlaw both done for the year and Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton still in his 21-day practice window, Washington is thin up front. Cowart reverted to the practice squad Monday; his Eagles elevation doesn’t automatically make him available against the Rams. The key in this coming game, and in the weeks ahead, is the Commanders establishing a rotation that can effectively stop the run, without getting gassed in the process.

title: Commanders News: Both Starting DTs Hit IR as Rams’ Matthew Stafford Deals With Arm Soreness | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
Tuesday made three more Commanders absences official. Daron Payne, Javon Kinlaw, and Jeremy McNichols went on injured reserve . Payne is out for the season; McNichols must miss at least four games. According to a report from Adam Schefter , Kinlaw underwent season-ending surgery Tuesday on his MCL. Robert Henry Jr. is back in Washington. The Commanders claimed him off waivers after Seattle waived him Monday to activate Jadarian Price. The Seahawks had signed Henry from Washington’s practice squad on October 6. Henry has yet to play in a regular-season NFL game, so his return gives Washington another option without settling who takes McNichols’ snaps. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler are the other backs on the active roster, with Devin Neal and Craig Reynolds still on the practice squad. Terry McLaurin was watching Sunday’s win from home, but his teammates made sure he was part of it. Jayden Daniels and Mike Sainristil wore shirts bearing his picture before the game. After Stefon Diggs scored, he joined Daniels, Antonio Williams and Josh Conerly Jr. at a camera for McLaurin’s “Scary Terry” celebration. Williams said the receivers wanted McLaurin to see it. The Rams had their own roster work Tuesday. They placed Dean Connors on injured reserve after he broke his hand against the Chargers, then waived Alex Bachman, who had handled nine punt returns and 13 kickoff returns this season. Kyren Williams and Blake Corum remain in the backfield. Bachman’s departure leaves Los Angeles with a punt return job to fill before Sunday. Los Angeles also signed Cam Lampkin from its practice squad to the active roster, brought Nyzier Fourqurean back to the practice squad and released linebacker Garrett Nelson from that unit. The cornerback move comes with Jaylen Watson’s shoulder and Trent McDuffie’s back under observation . Watson aggravated his injury against the Chargers. McVay said Monday that McDuffie felt better than expected, but neither player has an official Week 9 practice designation yet. Then there’s Matthew Stafford. He left Sunday’s game with ice on his right elbow, and McVay acknowledged soreness in his throwing arm. Ian Rapoport said Tuesday he expects Stafford to be ready for Washington . The Rams’ first injury report arrives Wednesday, when Stafford is also scheduled to speak with reporters.
Payne reportedly suffered a season-ending Jones fracture during Friday's practice, while McNichols is expected to miss significant time with a midfoot injury. Tim Settle Jr. and Shy Tuttle remain available at defensive tackle, although Washington could still look for additional help . Byron Cowart was elevated from the practice squad before the Philly game; he isn't automatically part of the active roster for the Rams game. Jer'Zhan Newton is still in his 21-day practice window and must be activated before he can play.
At 2-4-1, the Commanders have reasons to examine the interior offensive line, defensive tackle, and possibly running back before the November 10 trade deadline at 4 p.m. Eastern. Daron Payne's foot injury and the availability questions around Javon Kinlaw and Jer'Zhan Newton leave the defensive front short. Jeremy McNichols' midfoot injury could create another need, pending additional scans. The three pairings below are my proposals for how Peters could improve the roster this season.
We have claimed RB Robert Henry Jr. off waivers from Seattle pic.twitter.com/KrBsy1cjmu
While the Washington Commanders have struggled to stop opponents from getting explosive plays, they haven't been very successful at getting them either. That changed Sunday night. With 2:51 left in the third quarter, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels found receiver Treylon Burks for 53 yards, moving Washington from its own 40 to Philadelphia’s 7. It came exactly one play after Dorance Armstrong forced Tanner McKee’s fumble, which Charles Omenihu recovered, and it was the longest reception this season by a Commanders player.
Chig Okonkwo had only a 17.4 percent chance of catching his 21-yard reception in the third quarter against the Eagles, according to @ZebraTechnology . pic.twitter.com/2hik9kmqRO
Here's what we do know: the Commanders scored 27 unanswered points after that moment and took a 27-10 victory over the Eagles. No one said it publicly after the game, but Daniels' address to the offense served as an unofficial turning point during a night in which the Commanders needed a win. To the players, it was everything they expected from Daniels, who took another step in his development as a leader.
Players who worked out for Washington today: G Zack Johnson C  Doug Kramer C Michael  Niese G Brandon Walton
The penalties and miscues Washington’s coaching staff had vowed to clean up during the bye week continued to plague the team early as Washington’s offense had 4 penalties, 1 dropped pass, 1 fumble, and 1 missed field goal during the first three drives of Sunday night’s game. The Commanders would finish with 7 penalties for 50 yards in the first half, after simplifying their offense in an attempt to clean up the pre-snap mistakes. The NFL average for an entire game this season is right around eight per team.
Jayden Daniels is the only QB who has 100+ dropbacks without an interception this season 🎯 @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/9eXN3kGgzR

Meanwhile, Pro Football Talk moved the Commanders up six spots, and Sports Illustrated jumped them five. Same game, three very different opinions. title: Commanders Power Rankings Rise After Eagles Win, but One Writer Makes Bold NFC East Call
full_text:
Each week during the regular season, we'll look at what the national media is saying about the Washington Commanders via various publications' NFL Power Polls. With it being Week 9, seasons are starting to slip away around the league. The Washington Commanders finally gave the national media another win to work with, scoring 27 unanswered points Sunday night to beat the Philadelphia Eagles 27-10. That victory moved Washington to 2-4-1 and gave the team its first win since Week 3 against Seattle. Eight of the nine publications we track each week moved the Commanders up in their latest power rankings. Oddly enough, one actually dropped them two spots. * Side note: Many have asked whether these polls are helpful, which is a fair question. One way to look at them is as a way to broaden your perspective on what others believe. Not to mention, sometimes it's fun to see the national media guys bump around in the dark, chasing their tails, clueless.
Commanders Power Rankings - Week 9 (Average of 24)
Sports Illustrated - No. 22
Note : The table above links each poll to the corresponding publication name. Here's where things get interesting. Washington beat Philadelphia by 17 points, scored 27 unanswered, and somehow managed to drop two spots in NFL.com's rankings. Meanwhile, Pro Football Talk moved the Commanders up six spots, and Sports Illustrated jumped them five. Same game, three very different opinions. If you're wondering why I enjoy looking at these polls each week, there's a pretty good example. Then there's Sports Illustrated's Conor Orr, who has Washington at No. 22 and is already calling the Commanders his favorite to win the NFC East. That's quite a statement for a team sitting at 2-4-1, although beating Philadelphia the way Washington did certainly gives him something to work with. I'm not ready to go that far just yet. One good game doesn't erase everything we've watched over the first half of the season, but another win against the Rams on Sunday would make things a little more interesting. Orr also pointed to the connection between Daniels and Antonio Williams, and the rookie's snap counts against Philadelphia certainly back up the idea that his role is growing. Last week’s Power Ranking Index : No. 26 HIGHEST Ranking: No. 17 LOWEST Ranking: No. 27 Last week’s result : beat the Philadelphia Eagles 27-10 This week : vs. Los Angeles Rams ESPN had this to say (25th): Instead of a normal ranking blurb, ESPN inserted best in-season trades: This really is based on one season, as Muhammad played only two years for Washington. The franchise needed help after Art Monk was injured and traded a fourth-round pick to Oakland for the speedy Muhammad. In his 10 games with Washington in 1984, Muhammad caught 42 passes for 729 yards and four touchdowns. He was a key reason why, even without Monk, Washington's offense remained among the best in the NFL, ranking third in points and ninth in yards. A year later, with a healthy receiving group, Muhammad caught only nine passes and was released before the 1986 season. -- John Keim
CBS Sports had this to say (27th) Jayden Daniels won for the first time in a long time. They rallied to beat the Eagles as the offense showed life and the defense was better. Now here come the Rams. — Pete Prisco NFL.com had this to say (26th) Washington recorded a much-needed win over the lowly Eagles on Sunday night in a display that wasn’t pretty but counted the same as any other victory. It’s nice to see Treylon Burks find a role in this offense, and it’s good to watch Jayden Daniels pilot the unit effectively. It also didn’t tell me all that much about where this team stands at 2-4-1. — Nick Shook
Fox Sports had this to say (25th): The Commanders scored 27 unanswered points to beat a division rival on Sunday night, and ordinarily that would be cause for celebration. But the team they beat is the ghost of the Philadelphia Eagles, and it’s not like the Commanders needed much of an effort to do it. It certainly was a much-needed win for Dan Quinn , who miraculously managed to survive the bye week. He’ll need a lot more of those and a lot more from star QB Jayden Daniels , however, to keep his job after the season. And there are too many injuries and holes in the Commanders’ lineup to expect that. — Ralph Vacchiano Sports Illustrated had this to say (22nd): At this point in the race, Washington is my favorite to wind up winning the NFC East. Last night, the breadcrumbs shown between Jayden Daniels and Antonio Williams leads me to believe there’s just enough of a spark left in this offense to generate a run.   — Conor Orr
Yahoo Sports had this to say (23rd): Like everyone else in the NFC South and NFC East, other than the Eagles, the Commanders should feel like they have a shot to be division champions. The Commanders are flawed, without question, but sit just two games behind the Giants in the division. It's not like New York is a lock to run away with it. The biggest problem for the Commanders is the loss of receiver Terry McLaurin for the season. It leaves them thin at receiver, and the good news is there are a lot of veterans available at the deadline at various price points. The Commanders should be interested. They also should be interested in improving a secondary that ranks 27th in passing yards allowed.  — Frank Schwab Pro Football Talk had this to say (24th) Backward Hat Energy. — Mike Florio The Athletic had this to say (25th) The Commanders quarterback took a big hit from Nolan Smith on Sunday night that just added to what already has been a black-and-blue season. Daniels has only rushed for 33 yards (all on scrambles) in the last two weeks. If he’s not dynamic on the ground, he’s not the player Washington thought he was as a rookie, but that style of play is taking a toll. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Walter Football had this to say (17th) It's hard to believe that Jayden Daniels just won his first game of the year. I know he was out for a while, but it still feels like he probably should have won a game by now. However, that apparently hadn't happened. The win over Philadelphia was Washington's first victory since Week 3 against Seattle, which feels like a million years ago.
Put all nine together, and the Commanders land at an average ranking of No. 23.8, an improvement from last week's 26.2 . That's a decent jump for a team with only two wins, and Conor Orr at Sports Illustrated is already calling Washington his favorite to win the NFC East. Not everyone is convinced, though. Sunday's game against the Los Angeles Rams should give the national media another opportunity to decide how much that Eagles win was worth. title: Commanders Lose Three More Players to Injured Reserve Ahead of Rams Game
full_text:
NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Tuesday that the Washington Commanders are putting Jeremy McNichols, Daron Payne , and Javon Kinlaw on injured reserve, meaning all three will miss at least four games. Payne and Kinlaw missed Sunday night's game against Philadelphia, and McNichols hurt his foot during the game. Payne reportedly suffered a season-ending Jones fracture during Friday's practice, while McNichols is expected to miss significant time with a midfoot injury. Tim Settle Jr. and Shy Tuttle remain available at defensive tackle, although Washington could still look for additional help . Byron Cowart was elevated from the practice squad before the Philly game; he isn't automatically part of the active roster for the Rams game. Jer'Zhan Newton is still in his 21-day practice window and must be activated before he can play. What's really bad for McNichols here is that he just came back from IR after missing the first five weeks with a quadriceps injury; he can't seem to catch a break. With Jacory Croskey-Merritt also on IR with a groin injury, Washington had been down to Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler on its active roster. According to The Athletic, the Commanders claimed Robert Henry Jr. off waivers from Seattle on Tuesday, bringing back a player who was on their practice squad earlier this season. Devin Neal and Craig Reynolds remain practice-squad options. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn was worried that McNichols ' injury was serious, and was already looking ahead on Monday during his press conference: "It's definitely something that, once we go through the scans to see where we're at, we have some [backs] on practice squad as well." UPDATE : According to a report from Adam Schefter , Javon Kinlaw underwent season-ending surgery Tuesday on his MCL. title: 3 Players the Commanders Could Trade to Fill Bigger Roster Holes
full_text:
Mike Sainristil didn't play a defensive snap in the Washington Commanders ' 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday night. Commanders General Manager Adam Peters should be finding out what another team would give up for him. Washington has needs elsewhere, and using a player outside the defensive rotation to address one would make sense. At 2-4-1, the Commanders have reasons to examine the interior offensive line, defensive tackle, and possibly running back before the November 10 trade deadline at 4 p.m. Eastern. Daron Payne's foot injury and the availability questions around Javon Kinlaw and Jer'Zhan Newton leave the defensive front short. Jeremy McNichols' midfoot injury could create another need, pending additional scans. The three pairings below are my proposals for how Peters could improve the roster this season.
Washington's cornerback rotation against Philadelphia tells us where to start. Amik Robertson played 68 defensive snaps, Trey Amos played 60, and Rasul Douglas played 32. Dan Quinn also praised Nick Cross' work at nickel Monday. Mike Sainristil needs a path back into that group , but Peters has something another team might value: an experienced defensive back under contract through 2027, with a scheduled base salary of about $1.85 million next season. That gives Washington a reason to ask for a useful player in return. Jackson Powers-Johnson is one name I'd bring up. The Raiders have rotated him with Caleb Rogers at right guard, and he has starting experience at center and left guard. His rookie deal runs through 2027, giving Washington time to benefit if he earns a job inside. Las Vegas already has Taron Johnson, though, so Sainristil must have a role that interests the Raiders. I'd explore using him in an offer for Powers-Johnson, with compensation depending on how each team values the players. If the return is someone Washington would struggle to get on the field, I'd keep the affordable secondary depth.
Raiders iOL Jackson Powers-Johnson is playing out of position at OG with the Raiders. As a rookie, he played 6 games at C (288 pass block snaps) and allowed only 7 pressures while having a 67.2 pass block grade and a 66.5 run block grade per PFF. pic.twitter.com/3q9dZdw2Wd
Dyami Brown played 15 offensive snaps against the Eagles, or 25%, behind Antonio Williams, Treylon Burks, and Stefon Diggs . His contract ends after this season, making him a possible short-term addition for a team looking for speed at receiver. Washington still has to be careful here. Terry McLaurin is out for the year, and Burks spent last week dealing with a foot injury. Brown has a smaller role, but another injury could make those available snaps much more important. Kendre Miller is one name to examine. The Athletic's Jonathan Jones reported that New Orleans could move him. He has 159 rushing yards on 57 carries, a 2.8-yard average, and his contract also expires after this season. Brown would give the Saints another receiving option, but I don't see any benefit for Washington to make this move. Based on Miller's production, I'd keep the receiver depth unless the staff identifies a specific role Miller can fill better than the backs it already has.
Kendre Miller ain't going down. TD for 25 📺 FOX pic.twitter.com/4ILIHREgYE
Dorance Armstrong should require the most convincing offer. He played 40 defensive snaps, or 58%, against Philadelphia and finished with seven tackles, a sack, a forced fumble, and a tackle for loss. Washington would be removing production from a front that finally put together a strong game . His contract is scheduled to void in 2027, which gives Peters a reason to listen, but it doesn't make Armstrong expendable. I'd need an immediate improvement elsewhere to justify taking him out of this rotation. Christian Barmore is where that conversation could start. Sports Illustrated's Albert Breer reported that the Patriots defensive tackle could be available after playing 41.9% of New England's defensive snaps behind Milton Williams and Cory Durden. The Patriots list Dre'Mont Jones and Elijah Ponder as their edge starters, giving Peters a reason to ask whether Armstrong could be part of an offer. Barmore's cost matters, too. He's under contract through 2028, with scheduled base salaries of $18 million in 2027 and $19 million in 2028, before other payments. I'd pursue that discussion only if Washington sees a significant interior upgrade worth the future expense. New England would still have to value Armstrong enough to make the rest of the deal workable.
Christian Barmore sack drives em back. 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/xblB61RmST
Peters should be able to identify the incoming player's job before agreeing to a trade. Washington needs someone who can contribute immediately, and any return should justify the depth or production the Commanders would lose. title: Commanders Daily: How Washington Set Up Treylon Burks’ 53-Yard Catch Against the Eagles
full_text:
While the Washington Commanders have struggled to stop opponents from getting explosive plays, they haven't been very successful at getting them either. That changed Sunday night. With 2:51 left in the third quarter, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels found receiver Treylon Burks for 53 yards, moving Washington from its own 40 to Philadelphia’s 7. It came exactly one play after Dorance Armstrong forced Tanner McKee’s fumble, which Charles Omenihu recovered, and it was the longest reception this season by a Commanders player.
Former Arkansas Razorback Treylon Burks with a nice move on Quinyon Mitchell #NFL #SNF pic.twitter.com/0sKPUugAfF
Commanders head coach Dan Quinn pointed to Burks’ earlier second-quarter comeback route when discussing how one route can create an opportunity for a double-move later. "There was a deep comeback by Trey Burks. He ran it at about 24, 25 yards," Quinn said. "And it was a good throw, good rip on the comeback. And that is kind of the setup for a double move later that can go for a big pass. And so that’s kind of the back-and-forth that you work with in the passing game."
#Commanders Jayden Daniels was lethally accurate pushing the ball downfield, going 3/3 for 104 yards on passes that traveled 20+ yards in the air Treylon Burks came down with two and Antonio Williams had the other. Check it out #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/t8xphqD1SM
The play Quinn is referencing was a 21-yard pass from Daniels to Burks on second-and-6 that moved Washington from its own 15 to its 36. The comeback route (first play above) shows Burks pushing upfield before breaking back toward the sideline. A defender expecting that comeback can get caught moving forward when the receiver sells the same break and takes off downfield. That catch helped Washington’s 89-yard touchdown drive , which ended with Stefon Diggs’ eight-yard reception to tie the game at 10. Quinn also made it clear that Washington has to pick its spots. “If you get the specific looks that say, hey, here’s the chance to go put the ball up. Oftentimes, if you chase too much, you can get yourself into trouble. But when the moments are there, are you able to go nail them?” Quinn said. Burks finished with three catches for a team-high 81 yards, which Washington certainly needs with Terry McLaurin out for the season . The Commanders could have gotten more out of his biggest catch, though. After reaching Philadelphia’s 7, they gained nothing on their next three plays and settled for Drew Stevens’ 25-yard field goal to stretch the lead to 16-10. Getting Burks open downfield gave Washington a chance to put that game further out of reach. Against the Rams, the offense needs to finish more of those chances in the end zone.
